summaries.text: The [`target/app/__init__.py`](target/app/__init__.py) file is an empty package initializer that marks the `app` directory as a Python package [[target/app/__init__.py]]. It contains no definitions, imports, or logic of its own, serving solely to make `app` importable as a namespace for the modules within it [[target/app/__init__.py]].
This file is the package initialiser for the `app/api` module and contains no code of its own [[target/app/api/__init__.py]].

This file serves as the package initializer for the `api/dependencies` module, marking the directory as a Python package [[target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py]]. It contains no definitions of its own, but its presence makes the dependency components defined elsewhere in the package importable as a cohesive unit [[target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py]].

`check_article_modification_permissions` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]] is a FastAPI dependency function that enforces write-access control on an article. It accepts two injected parameters: `current_article`, resolved via `get_article_by_slug_from_path` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]], and `user`, resolved via `get_current_user_authorizer()` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. Both parameters are wired through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism, meaning the framework resolves them automatically before invoking the function [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. The function returns `None` on success — its sole job is to act as a guard [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. Internally it calls `check_user_can_modify_article` with the resolved article and user; if that check returns a falsy value, the function raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP status 403 Forbidden [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]]. Any route that declares this function as a dependency will therefore be blocked with a 403 response whenever the authenticated user is not the author of the targeted article [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::check_article_modification_permissions]].

`get_article_by_slug_from_path` is an asynchronous FastAPI dependency function that retrieves a single article by its URL slug [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. It accepts three injected parameters: a `slug` string drawn from the request path (enforced to be at least one character long), an optional `User` resolved via `get_current_user_authorizer(required=False)` so that unauthenticated callers are permitted [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]], and an `ArticlesRepository` instance supplied by `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. At runtime the function delegates to `articles_repo.get_article_by_slug`, passing both the slug and the (possibly absent) requesting user so that per-user state such as favouriting can be reflected in the result [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. If the repository signals that no matching article exists by raising `EntityDoesNotExist`, the function catches that exception and re-raises an `HTTPException` with a `404 Not Found` status code [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]. On success it returns the resolved `Article` object to whichever route handler declared this function as a dependency [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]].

`get_articles_filters` is a dependency function that collects query-string filter parameters for article listing and packages them into a single typed object [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. It accepts five optional inputs: `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` are plain `Optional[str]` values that default to `None`, while `limit` and `offset` are integers validated through FastAPI's `Query` helper — `limit` must be at least 1 and defaults to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT`, and `offset` must be at least 0 and defaults to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. The function constructs and returns an `ArticlesFilters` instance populated with all five values, making the assembled filter object available for injection into route handlers that need it [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_articles_filters]]. No exceptions are raised explicitly; constraint violations on `limit` or `offset` (such as a value below the declared minimum) are handled automatically by FastAPI's query validation before the function body is reached [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py]].

The `__call__` method is an asynchronous method defined on the `RWAPIKeyHeader` class that acts as the entry point when the dependency is invoked by FastAPI's dependency injection system [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. It accepts a `requests.Request` object as its sole non-self parameter and returns an `Optional[str]`, representing the extracted API key value if one is present [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]].

Its core logic delegates to the parent class implementation by calling `super().__call__(request)` with `await`, relying on Starlette's built-in API key header extraction behaviour [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. If the parent raises a `StarletteHTTPException` — which would occur when no valid API key header is found — the method catches it and re-raises a project-local `HTTPException`, substituting in a standardised authentication-required detail message rather than propagating the raw Starlette exception [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]]. This wrapping ensures that authentication failures surface with a consistent error shape aligned with the application's own exception handling conventions [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]]. The `# noqa: WPS610` comment suppresses a linter warning, which is an established pattern in this codebase for FastAPI dependency injection methods [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader::__call__]].

`_get_authorization_header` is a FastAPI dependency function that extracts and validates a Bearer token from an incoming HTTP request's authorization header [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. It accepts two injected parameters: `api_key`, a raw header string retrieved via `Security(RWAPIKeyHeader(...))`, and `settings`, the application configuration object supplied by `Depends(get_app_settings)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

The function attempts to split `api_key` on a single space into a prefix and a token [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. If the split does not yield exactly two parts — because no space is present or there are too many — a `ValueError` is caught and an `HTTPException` with status `403 Forbidden` is raised immediately [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. Even when the split succeeds, the extracted prefix is compared against `settings.jwt_token_prefix`; if they do not match, a second `403 Forbidden` `HTTPException` is raised with the same wrong-prefix detail message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

When both checks pass, the function returns the token portion of the header as a plain `str`, ready for downstream authentication logic [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]].

`_get_authorization_header_optional` is a FastAPI dependency function that optionally extracts and validates an authorization header from an incoming request [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. It accepts two injected parameters: `authorization`, an optional string pulled from the request via `Security(RWAPIKeyHeader(name=HEADER_KEY, auto_error=False))` which suppresses automatic errors when the header is absent, and `settings`, an `AppSettings` instance supplied by the `get_app_settings` dependency [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]] [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. When the `authorization` header is present, the function delegates to `_get_authorization_header`, passing both the raw header value and the application settings, and returns whatever that call produces [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. When no header is provided, the function returns an empty string rather than raising an error, making it suitable for endpoints where authentication is optional [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. In both cases the declared return type is `str` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]].

`_get_authorization_header_retriever` is a factory function that selects and returns one of two authorization-header retrieval callables based on whether the header is required [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. It accepts a single keyword-only argument, `required`, which defaults to `True` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. When `required` is `True` it returns `_get_authorization_header`, and when `False` it returns `_get_authorization_header_optional` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. The return type is annotated as `Callable`, suppressing the missing type-parameter warning with a `# type: ignore` comment [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]].

`_get_current_user` is an async dependency function that resolves the currently authenticated user from a JWT token, returning a [`User`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py) object [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

It accepts three injected parameters via FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. The `users_repo` parameter is a `UsersRepository` instance supplied by `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. The `token` string is extracted from the incoming request's authorization header by `_get_authorization_header_retriever` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. The `settings` parameter carries application configuration, including the secret key used to verify the token, and is provided by `get_app_settings` [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

The function first attempts to decode the JWT by calling `jwt.get_username_from_token`, passing the token and the application secret key obtained via `settings.secret_key.get_secret_value()` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. If the token is malformed or the decode fails with a `ValueError`, the function raises an `HTTPException` with a `403 Forbidden` status and a malformed-payload detail message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

If decoding succeeds, the function awaits `users_repo.get_user_by_username` to look up the user identified by the decoded username [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. If no matching user exists and an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception is raised by the repository, the function again raises an `HTTPException` with `403 Forbidden` and the same malformed-payload detail, preventing username enumeration [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. On success, the resolved `User` object is returned directly to the caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]].

`_get_current_user_optional` is an async dependency function that attempts to resolve the currently authenticated user, but treats authentication as optional and returns `None` when no credentials are present [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

It accepts three injected parameters via FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]]. The first is a `UsersRepository` instance, supplied by `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. The second is an optional bearer token string, retrieved by `_get_authorization_header_retriever` called with `required=False`, meaning no error is raised when the `Authorization` header is absent [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]]. The third is an `AppSettings` instance provided by `get_app_settings` [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

At runtime, if a token is present the function delegates to the internal `_get_current_user` helper, passing the repository, token, and settings, and returns the resolved `User` object [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]]. If the token is absent or falsy, the function returns `None` without attempting any lookup [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]]. The return type is therefore `Optional[User]`, reflecting both possible outcomes [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

`get_current_user_authorizer` is a factory function that selects and returns the appropriate authentication dependency based on whether authentication is required [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. It accepts a single keyword-only boolean parameter `required` (defaulting to `True`) and returns a `Callable` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. When `required` is `True`, it returns the strict authenticator (`_get_current_user`); when `False`, it returns the optional variant (`_get_current_user_optional`), allowing routes to declare whether an unauthenticated request should be rejected or tolerated [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The return type is annotated as `Callable` with a `# type: ignore` comment, indicating the precise callable signature is intentionally left unspecified to satisfy FastAPI's dependency injection system [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]].

`check_comment_modification_permissions` is a FastAPI dependency function that enforces write-access control on a comment, returning `None` on success and raising an `HTTPException` with a `403 Forbidden` status if the requesting user is not permitted to modify the comment [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

It accepts two injected arguments: a `Comment` object resolved by `get_comment_by_id_from_path`, and a `User` object resolved by `get_current_user_authorizer()`, both wired through FastAPI's `Depends` mechanism [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The resolved comment is the one identified by the path parameter of the enclosing route, and the resolved user is the currently authenticated caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

The function delegates the actual permission check to `check_user_can_modify_comment(comment, user)`; if that helper returns a falsy value, `HTTPException` is raised immediately with `HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN` and a detail string drawn from the `strings` module, preventing the route handler from executing [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]].

`get_comment_by_id_from_path` is an async FastAPI dependency function that retrieves a single comment by its ID, scoped to a specific article [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

It accepts four injected parameters: `comment_id`, an integer path parameter constrained to be at least 1; `article`, resolved by delegating to `get_article_by_slug_from_path` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]; `user`, an optionally authenticated caller resolved via `get_current_user_authorizer(required=False)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]; and `comments_repo`, a `CommentsRepository` instance provided through `get_repository` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

The function delegates the actual database lookup to `comments_repo.get_comment_by_id`, passing the resolved `comment_id`, `article`, and `user` [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. It returns a `Comment` on success [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. If the comment does not exist, the repository raises `EntityDoesNotExist`, which this function catches and converts into an HTTP 404 response by raising `fastapi.HTTPException` [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]].

`_get_connection_from_pool` is an asynchronous generator function defined in [`target/app/api/dependencies/database.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/database.py) that yields a single database connection for use within a request [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. It accepts one parameter, `pool`, a `Pool` instance that is resolved automatically via FastAPI's dependency injection using `_get_db_pool` as its source [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool]]. The function acquires a connection from that pool using `pool.acquire()` inside an `async with` block, then yields the resulting `Connection` object to the caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. Its return type is `AsyncGenerator[Connection, None]`, meaning it produces exactly one `Connection` and returns nothing after the generator is exhausted [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]]. Because `pool.acquire()` is used as an async context manager, the connection is automatically released back to the pool once the caller's scope exits, making this a safe and self-contained way to borrow a connection for the lifetime of a single request [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_connection_from_pool]].

`_get_db_pool` is a simple dependency helper that accepts a single [`request: Request`](target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool) parameter and returns the application-level database connection pool [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool]]. It retrieves the pool by reading `request.app.state.pool`, meaning the pool is expected to have been attached to the application's state object before any request is handled [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool]]. The return type is declared as `Pool` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::_get_db_pool]]. This function carries no decorators of its own and raises no exceptions directly; it is intended to be used as a FastAPI dependency that other route handlers or dependencies can declare to gain access to the shared pool [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py]].

`get_repository` is a factory function that, given a repository class, returns a FastAPI-compatible dependency function bound to that class [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. It accepts a single parameter, `repo_type`, typed as `Type[BaseRepository]`, which specifies which repository class should be instantiated [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. Its return type is `Callable[[Connection], BaseRepository]`, meaning it produces a callable that takes a database connection and yields a repository instance [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

The inner function `_get_repo` uses FastAPI's `Depends` to receive a `Connection` from the connection pool, then constructs and returns an instance by calling `repo_type(conn)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. Because the outer function closes over `repo_type`, each call to `get_repository` with a different class produces an independent, correctly-typed dependency resolver [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]]. The file itself houses this pattern as the primary mechanism for injecting database-backed repositories into route handlers [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py]].

`get_profile_by_username_from_path` is an asynchronous FastAPI dependency function that looks up a user profile by username and returns it to the caller [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]].

It accepts three injected parameters: a `username` string extracted from the URL path (enforced to be at least one character long via `Path`), an optional `User` object representing the currently authenticated caller (which may be `None` when no credentials are supplied), and a `ProfilesRepository` instance used to query the data store [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]]. The optional current user is resolved through `get_current_user_authorizer` called with `required=False`, meaning authentication is permitted but not mandatory [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The repository is provided via `get_repository`, which handles database session injection [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

The function delegates the actual database lookup to `profiles_repo.get_profile_by_username`, passing both the target `username` and the `requested_user` so that the repository can resolve follow relationships or other viewer-relative data [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]]. On success it returns a `Profile` object [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]]. If the repository raises an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception because no matching user is found, the function catches it and raises an `HTTPException` with a `404 Not Found` status code instead [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]].
This module is an empty initializer that marks the `errors` directory as a Python package [[target/app/api/errors/__init__.py]].

`http_error_handler` is an asynchronous function that serves as an HTTP exception handler, converting Starlette `HTTPException` instances into structured JSON responses [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py::http_error_handler]]. It accepts two parameters: an unnamed `Request` object (ignored, indicated by the `_` convention) and an `HTTPException` named `exc` [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py::http_error_handler]]. It returns a `JSONResponse` whose body is a JSON object with a single `"errors"` key mapped to a list containing `exc.detail`, and whose HTTP status code is taken directly from `exc.status_code` [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py::http_error_handler]]. This design ensures that any HTTP error raised in the application is surfaced to the client in a consistent envelope format rather than as a plain text or default framework response [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py]].

`http422_error_handler` is an asynchronous function that handles HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity errors by converting validation exceptions into a structured JSON response [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]].

It accepts two parameters: a `Request` object (unused, indicated by the `_` name) and an `exc` argument typed as either a `RequestValidationError` or a `ValidationError` [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]]. The function calls `exc.errors()` to retrieve the list of validation error details and wraps them under an `"errors"` key [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]]. It then returns a `JSONResponse` with that payload and a status code of `HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY` [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]].
This is an empty module that serves as a package initialiser for the `app.api.routes` namespace, containing no definitions of its own [[target/app/api/routes/__init__.py]].

This module serves as the top-level API router that assembles all feature-specific sub-routers into a single unified router for the application [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. It creates a root `APIRouter` instance and registers six sub-routers onto it, each bound to a specific URL prefix and tagged for grouping in the generated API schema [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. The authentication routes are mounted under `/users`, user profile management routes under `/user`, and profiles under `/profiles` [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. Article routes are included without an additional prefix, while comment routes are nested under `/articles/{slug}/comments` to reflect their relationship to a specific article identified by its slug [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. Tag routes are mounted under `/tags`, completing the full surface of the API [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. The articles sub-router is sourced from a nested `api` module within the `articles` package, while all other sub-routers are imported directly from their respective sibling modules [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]].

The [`__init__.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py) file serves as the package initializer for the `articles` route module, marking the directory as a Python package [[target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py]]. As an empty initializer, it contains no definitions of its own, but its presence makes the `articles` directory importable as part of the broader API routing structure [[target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py]].

This module serves as the top-level assembly point for the articles section of the API, creating a single `APIRouter` instance and mounting two sub-routers under the `/articles` URL prefix [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]]. It imports `articles_common` and `articles_resource` from the same package and delegates their routes into the combined router, meaning all article-related endpoints — both shared/common logic and resource-specific operations — are unified here before being registered with the broader application [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]].

`get_articles_for_user_feed` is an asynchronous route handler registered on `GET /api/articles/feed` that returns a paginated list of articles tailored to the authenticated user's feed [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]] [[route:GET /api/articles/feed]].

It accepts two optional integer query parameters, `limit` and `offset`, both validated with FastAPI's `Query` — `limit` must be at least 1 and `offset` at least 0, with default values drawn from module-level constants [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. Authentication is enforced through the `user` parameter, which is resolved by injecting `get_current_user_authorizer()` via FastAPI's `Depends` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]. The repository used to query articles is likewise injected by `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

Inside the handler, it awaits a call to `articles_repo.get_articles_for_user_feed`, passing the resolved `user`, `limit`, and `offset` to retrieve only the articles relevant to that user [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. Each returned article is then converted into an `ArticleForResponse` instance by unpacking the article's fields as a dictionary [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. The handler wraps the resulting list and its count into a `ListOfArticlesInResponse` object, which is also the declared `response_model` on the route decorator, and returns it [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]].

`mark_article_as_favorite` is an async POST endpoint registered at `/api/articles/{slug}/favorite` that allows an authenticated user to mark a specific article as a favourite [[route:POST /api/articles/{slug}/favorite]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]].

It is decorated with `router.post("/{slug}/favorite", response_model=ArticleInResponse, name="articles:mark-article-favorite")`, which registers the route and declares that successful responses conform to the `ArticleInResponse` schema [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]].

The function accepts three injected dependencies: the target `Article`, resolved from the URL's `{slug}` path parameter via `get_article_by_slug_from_path` [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py::get_article_by_slug_from_path]]; the currently authenticated `User`, supplied by `get_current_user_authorizer()` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]]; and an `ArticlesRepository` instance for database access, provided by `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py::get_repository]].

When the article has not yet been favourited by the user, the function calls `articles_repo.add_article_into_favorites` to persist the relationship, then constructs and returns an `ArticleInResponse` whose embedded `ArticleForResponse` reflects the updated state — `favorited` set to `True` and `favorites_count` incremented by one — without re-querying the database, using `article.copy` to produce the updated view [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]].

If the article is already favourited (`article.favorited` is truthy), the function raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 400, signalling that the article has already been added to the user's favourites [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]]. The function begins by copying `jwt_content` so the caller's original dictionary is not mutated [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]]. It then computes an expiry timestamp by adding `expires_delta` to the current UTC time [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]]. A `JWTMeta` object is constructed with that expiry and a fixed `JWT_SUBJECT` value, converted to a plain dictionary, and merged into the working copy of the claims [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]]. It works by calling `jwt.decode` with the provided `token` and `secret_key`, passing a fixed signing algorithm, and then unpacking the resulting dictionary into a `JWTUser` model to extract the `username` field [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]]. The second handler, `mark_article_as_favorite`, is mounted on `POST /{slug}/favorite` and allows an authenticated user to favourite a specific article [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]]. When the article has not yet been favourited, it persists the relationship and returns an `ArticleInResponse` whose embedded `ArticleForResponse` reflects `favorited` set to `True` and `favorites_count` incremented by one, computed in-memory with `article.copy` rather than a second database round-trip [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]]. If the article is already favourited, the handler raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 400 [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]].

The third handler, `remove_article_from_favorites`, is the mirror image of the second, mounted on `DELETE /{slug}/favorite` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. It resolves the same three dependencies and checks whether the article is currently favourited [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. If it is, it awaits the repository removal and returns an `ArticleInResponse` with `favorited` set to `False` and `favorites_count` decremented by one [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. If the article was not favourited to begin with, it raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 400 [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]].

All three handlers share the same dependency resolution pattern — authentication via `get_current_user_authorizer()` and database access via `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` — and the two favouriting handlers additionally share slug-based article resolution via `get_article_by_slug_from_path`, making the module a cohesive set of related article-feed and favouriting endpoints built on a common injection foundation [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]].

This module defines the FastAPI router and all five route handlers that together form the articles REST API [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]]. A single `APIRouter` instance named `router` is declared at module level and each handler is attached to it via decorator, so the full set of CRUD operations for articles lives in one place [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]].

The `list_articles` handler serves `GET /api/articles` and accepts optional filtering and pagination parameters — tag, author, favorited, limit, and offset — alongside an optionally authenticated user, delegating the actual database query to `ArticlesRepository.filter_articles` before returning a `ListOfArticlesInResponse` envelope containing the converted articles and their count [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]]. Authentication is optional on this endpoint, meaning unauthenticated callers can still retrieve articles, though the repository may tailor results when a user identity is present [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]].

The `create_new_article` handler serves `POST /api/articles` and requires an authenticated user [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]]. It derives a URL slug from the submitted title and checks for a duplicate before writing; if a conflicting slug is found it raises an HTTP 400 error before any persistence occurs, otherwise it delegates to `articles_repo.create_article` and returns the newly created article wrapped in an `ArticleInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]].

The `retrieve_article_by_slug` handler serves `GET /api/articles/{slug}` and contains no lookup logic of its own — the article is fully resolved from the path segment by the `get_article_by_slug_from_path` dependency before the handler body runs, and the handler simply converts the injected ORM object into an `ArticleInResponse` via `ArticleForResponse.from_orm` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]].

The `update_article_by_slug` handler serves `PUT /api/articles/{slug}` and shares the same slug-resolution dependency as the retrieval handler, receiving the existing article ready to use [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. Both this handler and `delete_article_by_slug` declare `check_article_modification_permissions` as a route-level dependency in their decorators, so FastAPI enforces the authorisation check before either handler body executes [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]]. When a new title is supplied, `update_article_by_slug` recomputes the slug from it; all fields from the update payload are then spread as keyword arguments into `articles_repo.update_article`, and the result is returned as an `ArticleInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]].

The `delete_article_by_slug` handler serves `DELETE /api/articles/{slug}`, responds with HTTP 204 No Content, and its entire body is a single awaited call to `articles_repo.delete_article` with the resolved article, returning `None` afterwards [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]].

This module defines the authentication routes for the API, exposing two POST endpoints that handle user login and registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py]]. It creates a single `APIRouter` instance that both handlers are attached to, and all authentication-related HTTP traffic flows through this file [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py]].

The `login` function handles credential verification for existing users [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. It receives the submitted email and password from the request body, looks up the matching user record via the injected `UsersRepository`, and raises an HTTP 400 error if either the email is not found or the password fails verification [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. On success, it mints a JWT access token using the application secret key and returns the user's profile data bundled with that token in a `UserInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]].

The `register` function handles the creation of new user accounts [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]]. Before persisting anything, it runs two uniqueness checks against the repository — one for the requested username and one for the requested email — raising an HTTP 400 error if either is already taken [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]]. If both checks pass, it delegates record creation to `users_repo.create_user`, then immediately mints a JWT access token for the new user using the same approach as `login`, and returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping a `UserWithToken` so the caller is authenticated from the moment of registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

The two handlers share the same structural pattern: both accept a `UsersRepository` and `AppSettings` via FastAPI dependency injection, and both produce a `UserInResponse` containing a `UserWithToken` — meaning the token-issuance logic is symmetric across login and registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

This module is the FastAPI router that handles all comment-related HTTP endpoints for articles, defining three route handlers mounted on a shared `APIRouter` instance [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py]].

`list_comments_for_article` services `GET /api/articles/{slug}/comments` and returns every comment associated with the article identified by the URL slug [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::list_comments_for_article]]. The article is resolved from the path via a shared dependency, and the caller may be either authenticated or anonymous — authentication is optional at this endpoint [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::list_comments_for_article]]. The handler delegates to the repository and wraps the result in a `ListOfCommentsInResponse` before returning it to the caller [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::list_comments_for_article]].

`create_comment_for_article` services `POST /api/articles/{slug}/comments` and responds with HTTP 201 on success [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::create_comment_for_article]]. Unlike the listing endpoint, it requires a fully authenticated user; the comment body is taken from the request payload under the key `"comment"`, the target article is resolved from the path slug, and persistence is delegated to the `CommentsRepository` [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::create_comment_for_article]]. The newly persisted comment is returned serialised as a `CommentInResponse` [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::create_comment_for_article]].

`delete_comment_from_article` services `DELETE /api/articles/{slug}/comments/{comment_id}` and responds with HTTP 204 No Content, returning no body [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::delete_comment_from_article]]. Before the handler body runs, a route-level dependency enforces that the caller is authorised to modify the target comment; the comment itself is resolved from the path's `{comment_id}` segment, and the handler delegates removal to the repository with a single awaited call [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::delete_comment_from_article]].

All three handlers share the same structural pattern: article and comment objects are resolved through path-based dependencies, database access flows through a `CommentsRepository` injected via `get_repository`, and authentication state is obtained through the same authoriser dependency — configured as required or optional depending on the operation [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py]].

This module defines the FastAPI router for user profile operations, exposing three HTTP endpoints under the `/api/profiles/` prefix [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py]]. A single `APIRouter` instance groups all three handlers, which together cover reading a profile, following a user, and unfollowing a user [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py]].

The `retrieve_profile_by_username` handler responds to `GET /{username}` and is the simplest of the three: it accepts a `Profile` object already resolved from the URL path segment by the `get_profile_by_username_from_path` dependency, wraps it in a `ProfileInResponse` envelope, and returns it immediately without any additional logic [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::retrieve_profile_by_username]]. Any failure due to an unknown username surfaces from that dependency before the handler body is ever reached [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::retrieve_profile_by_username]].

The `follow_for_user` handler responds to `POST /{username}/follow` and requires an authenticated caller [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]]. In addition to the resolved `Profile`, it injects the current `User` and a `ProfilesRepository` for database access [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]]. It enforces two guard conditions before writing anything: it rejects the request with HTTP 400 if the caller and target share the same username, and it rejects it again with HTTP 400 if the profile is already being followed [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]]. When both guards pass, it calls `profiles_repo.add_user_into_followers` to persist the relationship, then returns a `ProfileInResponse` carrying a copy of the profile with `following` forced to `True` [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]].

The `unsubscribe_from_user` handler is the mirror of `follow_for_user`, responding to `DELETE /{username}/follow` [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::unsubscribe_from_user]]. It injects the same three dependencies and applies the same self-referential guard, but its second guard checks the opposite condition — it raises HTTP 400 if the caller is *not* currently following the target [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::unsubscribe_from_user]]. If both guards pass, it calls `profiles_repo.remove_user_from_followers` to persist the unfollow, then returns a `ProfileInResponse` with `following` explicitly set to `False` [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::unsubscribe_from_user]].

All three handlers share the same response shape — `ProfileInResponse` — which FastAPI also uses to generate the OpenAPI schema for each route [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py]].

The module [`target/app/api/routes/tags.py`](target/app/api/routes/tags.py) is a FastAPI router file responsible for exposing tag-related HTTP endpoints [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py]]. It defines a single `APIRouter` instance and registers one route handler on it [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py]].

The only function defined in this module is [`get_all_tags`](target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags), an asynchronous route handler bound to `GET /api/tags` [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags]]. It receives a `TagsRepository` instance through FastAPI's dependency injection mechanism, delegating the database wiring to `get_repository(TagsRepository)` so the handler itself never constructs its own database connection [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags]]. The handler awaits `tags_repo.get_all_tags()` to fetch all tags from the data store, then wraps the result in a `TagsInList` instance which is both the return value and the declared response model governing JSON serialisation [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags]]. No authentication or authorisation decorators are applied, meaning the endpoint is publicly accessible as written, and no exceptions are explicitly raised within the function body [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py]].

This module defines the FastAPI router for the authenticated user resource, exposing two endpoints that allow a logged-in user to retrieve and update their own profile [[target/app/api/routes/users.py]].

The `retrieve_current_user` handler is registered on `GET ""` (resolved to `GET /api/user` by the application's route prefix) and returns the current user's profile together with a freshly minted JWT access token [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::retrieve_current_user]]. It depends on `get_current_user_authorizer()` to resolve the authenticated `User` and on `get_app_settings` to obtain the secret key used when calling `jwt.create_access_token_for_user`, then wraps the result in a `UserInResponse` containing a `UserWithToken` [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::retrieve_current_user]].

The `update_current_user` handler is registered on `PUT ""` (resolved to `PUT /api/user`) and performs a guarded profile update before returning the same kind of response [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]]. It accepts a `UserInUpdate` request body (embedded under the JSON key `"user"`), the authenticated `User`, a `UsersRepository` for database access, and application settings [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]]. Before touching the database, it runs two uniqueness checks: if the incoming username differs from the current one and is already taken, it raises an `HTTPException` with HTTP 400; it applies the same guard to the incoming email address [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]]. Only when both checks pass does it call `users_repo.update_user` to persist the changes, after which it mints a new token and returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping the updated `UserWithToken` [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]].

The two handlers share a common response shape — `UserInResponse` containing `UserWithToken` — and both issue a fresh JWT on every successful request, ensuring the token in the response always reflects the current state of the user record [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::retrieve_current_user]] [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]].

This module serves as the central configuration entry point for the application, mapping environment identifiers to their corresponding settings classes and exposing a single cached accessor for the active configuration [[target/app/core/config.py]]. It defines an `environments` dictionary that associates each `AppEnvTypes` variant — `dev`, `prod`, and `test` — with the matching settings class (`DevAppSettings`, `ProdAppSettings`, or `TestAppSettings` respectively) [[target/app/core/config.py]].

The sole function defined here, `get_app_settings`, acts as a cached factory: it reads the current environment from `BaseAppSettings`, looks up the appropriate class in the `environments` mapping, instantiates it, and returns the resulting `AppSettings` object [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. Because it is decorated with `@lru_cache`, this resolution happens only once per process lifetime — every subsequent call receives the same cached instance without re-reading the environment [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]]. The function takes no parameters and its return type is declared as `AppSettings` [[target/app/core/config.py::get_app_settings]].

[`target/app/core/events.py`](target/app/core/events.py) is a module responsible for wiring up the application's database lifecycle — specifically, producing the startup and shutdown handlers that connect to and disconnect from the database at the appropriate moments in a FastAPI application's lifecycle [[target/app/core/events.py]].

The module exposes two factory functions. `create_start_app_handler` accepts a `FastAPI` instance and an `AppSettings` configuration object and returns a `Callable` [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]]. The callable it returns is an async function that, when invoked, calls `connect_to_db` with the application and settings, establishing the database connection [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]]. By closing over both arguments at construction time, the handler defers the actual connection work until the application starts up [[target/app/core/events.py]].

The companion function, `create_stop_app_handler`, accepts only a `FastAPI` instance and returns a `Callable` suited for registration as an on-shutdown handler [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]]. The inner async function it produces is decorated with `@logger.catch`, which intercepts and logs any exceptions raised during teardown, and calls `close_db_connection` with the application instance to cleanly close the database connection [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]].

Together, the two factory functions follow the same structural pattern: each captures its arguments in a closure, builds an async inner callable that performs the real work, and returns that callable for the application to register on its startup and shutdown hooks [[target/app/core/events.py::create_start_app_handler]] [[target/app/core/events.py::create_stop_app_handler]].

[`InterceptHandler`](target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler) is a concrete subclass of the standard library's `logging.Handler`, defined in [`target/app/core/logging.py`](target/app/core/logging.py) [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. It is not a Pydantic model [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. Its sole responsibility is to act as a bridge between Python's built-in logging system and Loguru, intercepting every log record emitted through the standard `logging` API and routing it into Loguru for unified handling [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

The class defines no fields of its own, inheriting whatever state `logging.Handler` provides, and its entire behaviour is expressed through a single overridden method, [`emit`](target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit) [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. That method accepts a `logging.LogRecord` and returns `None`, fulfilling the abstract contract required by `logging.Handler` [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit]]. It first translates the record's level name into a Loguru-native level by calling `logger.level`; if the level is unknown to Loguru and a `ValueError` is raised, it falls back to the raw integer level number converted to a string [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit]]. It then walks the call stack, advancing past any frames whose source file belongs to the `logging` module itself, so that Loguru reports the true originating call site rather than an internal logging frame [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit]]. Finally, it calls `logger.opt` with the computed stack depth and the record's `exc_info`, then dispatches the event to Loguru via `.log` with the resolved level and the message from `record.getMessage` [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit]]. The method carries a `# pragma: no cover` marker, indicating it is intentionally excluded from code-coverage measurement [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler::emit]].

`AppSettings` is a Pydantic model that serves as the central configuration class for the application, extending `BaseAppSettings` to add all runtime settings needed by the web server, database, authentication, and logging subsystems [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]] [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]].

Its fields cover four broad concerns. For the FastAPI application itself, it declares `debug` (default `False`), `docs_url` (default `"/docs"`), `openapi_prefix` (default `""`), `openapi_url` (default `"/openapi.json"`), `redoc_url` (default `"/redoc"`), `title` (default `"FastAPI example application"`), and `version` (default `"0.0.0"`) [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For the database, it requires a `database_url` of type `PostgresDsn` with no default, and accepts `max_connection_count` and `min_connection_count`, both `int` defaulting to `10` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For authentication, it requires a `secret_key` of type `SecretStr`, an `api_prefix` defaulting to `"/api"`, a `jwt_token_prefix` defaulting to `"Token"`, and an `allowed_hosts` list defaulting to `["*"]` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For logging, it holds `logging_level` (default `logging.INFO`) and `loggers`, a two-element `Tuple[str, str]` defaulting to `("uvicorn.asgi", "uvicorn.access")` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The inner `Config` class enables `validate_assignment`, meaning Pydantic enforces type constraints whenever a field is updated after construction [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. It also inherits `app_env` of type `AppEnvTypes` (defaulting to `AppEnvTypes.prod`) from `BaseAppSettings` [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]].

The class exposes two behaviours. The `fastapi_kwargs` read-only property packages the seven FastAPI-relevant fields — `debug`, `docs_url`, `openapi_prefix`, `openapi_url`, `redoc_url`, `title`, and `version` — into a plain `Dict[str, Any]` that can be unpacked directly into the FastAPI constructor, without calling any external functions or producing side effects [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings::fastapi_kwargs]]. The `configure_logging` method wires up the application's logging infrastructure by routing both the root logger and each logger named in `self.loggers` through Loguru's `InterceptHandler`, and then establishes a Loguru sink writing to `sys.stderr` at `self.logging_level`, so that all intercepted records are ultimately handled in one place [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings::configure_logging]].

This module establishes the foundational configuration layer for the application by defining two classes that work together [[target/app/core/settings/base.py]]. `AppEnvTypes` is a standard Python `Enum` that enumerates the three deployment environments the application recognises — `prod`, `dev`, and `test` — each carrying a matching string value [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::AppEnvTypes]]. `BaseAppSettings` is a Pydantic `BaseSettings` subclass that acts as the root configuration class from which environment-specific settings classes are intended to inherit [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]]. Because it extends `BaseSettings`, it can automatically populate field values from environment variables or a `.env` file, as declared in its inner `Config` class [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]]. The two classes are directly coupled: `BaseAppSettings` declares a single field, `app_env`, typed as `AppEnvTypes` with a default of `AppEnvTypes.prod`, meaning the application assumes a production context unless the environment explicitly overrides it [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]] [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::AppEnvTypes]].

The [`development.py`](target/app/core/settings/development.py) module defines the development-environment configuration for the FastAPI application by providing a single class, `DevAppSettings` [[target/app/core/settings/development.py]].

[`DevAppSettings`](target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings) is a Pydantic model that extends `AppSettings` to supply development-specific overrides [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]]. It sets `debug` to `True`, gives the application the title `"Dev FastAPI example application"`, and raises `logging_level` to `logging.DEBUG` so that verbose log output is emitted during local development [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]]. Its inner `Config` class subclasses `AppSettings.Config` and points `env_file` to `".env"`, which causes Pydantic to load environment variables from that file when the application runs in development mode [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]].

Beyond those overrides, `DevAppSettings` inherits the complete set of fields from `AppSettings` [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]]. Those inherited fields cover database connectivity (`database_url`, `max_connection_count`, `min_connection_count`), security (`secret_key`, `jwt_token_prefix`), API routing (`api_prefix`, `openapi_prefix`, `openapi_url`, `docs_url`, `redoc_url`), network access (`allowed_hosts`), logging targets (`loggers`), versioning (`version`), and the active environment indicator `app_env` [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]].

This module defines the production configuration layer for the application [[target/app/core/settings/production.py]]. It contains a single class, `ProdAppSettings`, which extends `AppSettings` to provide production-specific settings [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]].

`ProdAppSettings` is a Pydantic model that inherits all fields from `AppSettings` without modification, adding only a nested `Config` class that overrides `env_file` to point at `prod.env`, so that environment variables are sourced from that file at runtime [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. Through inheritance, it carries FastAPI application metadata such as `title`, `version`, `docs_url`, `openapi_url`, `redoc_url`, and `openapi_prefix` [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. Database connectivity is governed by `database_url` (a `PostgresDsn`), `max_connection_count`, and `min_connection_count` [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. Security is handled via `secret_key` (a `SecretStr`) and `jwt_token_prefix` [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. Routing is controlled by `api_prefix` and `allowed_hosts`, while logging behaviour is set through `logging_level` and `loggers` [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. The `app_env` field defaults to `AppEnvTypes.prod`, which identifies this class as the active settings object when the application runs in production [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]].

This module defines the test-environment configuration for the FastAPI application [[target/app/core/settings/test.py]]. It contains a single class, `TestAppSettings`, which extends `AppSettings` and overrides a focused set of fields with values designed for automated testing [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

`TestAppSettings` is a Pydantic model that fixes several settings to make test runs deterministic and self-contained [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]]. The `debug` flag is enabled and `title` is set to `"Test FastAPI example application"`, clearly marking the running instance as a test build [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]]. The `secret_key` is hardcoded to the literal `SecretStr("test_secret")`, ensuring that any cryptographic operations produce consistent, reproducible results across all test runs [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]]. Both `max_connection_count` and `min_connection_count` are capped at `5`, keeping the database connection pool deliberately small during testing [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]]. The `logging_level` is set to `logging.DEBUG` so that the full log output is available when diagnosing test failures [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

One field is intentionally left without a default: `database_url`, typed as `PostgresDsn`, must be supplied externally — for example via an environment variable — even in the test environment [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]]. All remaining fields (`docs_url`, `openapi_prefix`, `openapi_url`, `redoc_url`, `version`, `api_prefix`, `jwt_token_prefix`, `allowed_hosts`, `loggers`, and `app_env`) are inherited from `AppSettings` without modification [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

This module serves as the errors definition layer for the database package, providing a dedicated place to declare database-specific exception types [[target/app/db/errors.py]]. It defines a single class, `EntityDoesNotExist`, which inherits directly from Python's built-in `Exception` and adds no extra fields or methods of its own [[target/app/db/errors.py::EntityDoesNotExist]]. Its sole responsibility, as declared in its docstring, is to be raised whenever a requested entity cannot be located in the database [[target/app/db/errors.py::EntityDoesNotExist]].

[`target/app/db/events.py`](target/app/db/events.py) is a small lifecycle module responsible for managing the PostgreSQL connection pool used by the FastAPI application [[target/app/db/events.py]]. It defines exactly two async functions — `connect_to_db` and `close_db_connection` — which together form a matched pair: one to open the pool at startup and one to shut it down on exit [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]].

[`connect_to_db()`](target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db) accepts a `FastAPI` application instance and an `AppSettings` configuration object, uses them to call `asyncpg.create_pool` with the database URL and the configured minimum and maximum connection counts, and stores the resulting pool on `app.state.pool` so the rest of the application can reach it for the lifetime of the process [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]]. [`close_db_connection()`](target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection) is the counterpart: it takes only the `FastAPI` instance, awaits `app.state.pool.close()` to tear down that same pool, and returns `None` [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]].

Both functions are `async` and must be awaited by the caller, making them natural fits for FastAPI's startup and shutdown lifecycle event hooks [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]]. Each function also brackets its work with a pair of `loguru` log messages — one before the operation begins and one after it completes — providing an observable trace of connection pool activity in application logs [[target/app/db/events.py::connect_to_db]] [[target/app/db/events.py::close_db_connection]].

The class declares a single class-level field, `__table__`, initialised to an empty string, which subclasses can override to specify the target database table name without passing it explicitly at construction time [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]]. No additional instance fields beyond those inherited from `Table` are introduced [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]].

Its constructor accepts four optional parameters — `name`, `schema`, `alias`, and `query_cls` — all defaulting to `None` [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable::__init__]]. When `name` is omitted, it applies a two-step fallback: it uses the value of `__table__` if that attribute is set on the class, and otherwise falls back to the class's own `__name__` [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable::__init__]]. The overall responsibility of `TypedTable` is therefore to let subclasses act as self-describing table references: a subclass needs only to set `__table__` (or rely on its own class name) and the correct table identity is resolved automatically at construction time [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]] [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable::__init__]].

`ArticlesRepository` is the data-access class responsible for all database operations involving articles, spanning creation, retrieval, filtering, updating, deletion, and favourites management [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. It is not a Pydantic model; it is a plain Python class that inherits from [`BaseRepository`](target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository), which supplies the shared database connection infrastructure used throughout [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]].

The constructor accepts a `Connection` object, passes it to the parent via `super().__init__(conn)`, and additionally instantiates two collaborating repositories — `ProfilesRepository` and `TagsRepository` — each sharing the same connection, stored as `self._profiles_repo` and `self._tags_repo` [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::__init__]]. This means the class holds no independently declared data fields; its only instance state is the connection inherited from the base class and those two sub-repository references [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::__init__]].

The public write surface covers four operations. `create_article` persists a new article within a database transaction, optionally upserts any supplied tags via `_tags_repo`, links them to the article via the private `_link_article_with_tags` helper, and then hydrates a full `Article` domain object from the raw row [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::create_article]]. `update_article` deep-copies the existing `Article`, applies whichever of the four optional field overrides (`slug`, `title`, `body`, `description`) were provided, executes the update inside a transaction, and returns the copy with its `updated_at` field set to the timestamp returned by the database [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::update_article]]. `delete_article` wraps the removal of the article row in a transaction, using the article's slug and author username as lookup keys [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::delete_article]]. `add_article_into_favorites` and `remove_article_from_favorites` each delegate directly to the corresponding named query, translating the `Article` and `User` domain objects into the slug and username identifiers the query layer expects [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::add_article_into_favorites]] [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::remove_article_from_favorites]].

The public read surface covers five operations. `get_article_by_slug` fetches a single raw row by slug and raises `EntityDoesNotExist` if none is found, otherwise delegating to the private assembly helper [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::get_article_by_slug]]. `filter_articles` dynamically builds a pypika query, conditionally joining `articles_to_tags`, `users`, and `favorites` when the `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` filter arguments are respectively supplied, appending `limit` and `offset` as positional asyncpg parameters, and converting each resulting row into an `Article` [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::filter_articles]]. `get_articles_for_user_feed` queries for articles authored by users that the requesting user follows, paginating with `limit` and `offset` and hydrating each row in the same manner [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. `get_tags_for_article_by_slug` returns a plain `List[str]` extracted from the tag rows for a given slug [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::get_tags_for_article_by_slug]]. `get_favorites_count_for_article_by_slug` returns an `int` by querying the database and extracting the `"favorites_count"` field [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::get_favorites_count_for_article_by_slug]]. `is_article_favorited_by_user` returns a `bool` indicating whether a specific user has favourited a specific article, delegating to a named query and extracting the `"favorited"` key [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::is_article_favorited_by_user]].

Two private helpers support the public API. `_get_article_from_db_record` is the central assembly point: it reads scalar fields directly from the raw database `Record`, then performs additional async calls to fetch the author's profile (with follow-state relative to `requested_user`), the article's tags, the favourites count, and — only when `requested_user` is present — the per-user favourited flag, defaulting to `False` for unauthenticated callers [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::_get_article_from_db_record]]. `_link_article_with_tags` constructs a list of `{slug, tag}` dictionaries and passes it to `queries.add_tags_to_article`, serving exclusively as an internal helper for write operations that need to associate tags with an article [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository::_link_article_with_tags]].

It returns the result of `user.copy(update=dict(user_row))`, merging any server-generated values such as an auto-assigned id or timestamps back onto the in-memory model [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::create_user]].

It first fetches the current database state via `get_user_by_username`, merges each provided field using a short-circuit `or` so that absent arguments leave stored values unchanged, and, when a new password is supplied, derives fresh salt and hash values before writing [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::update_user]]. The entire database write is wrapped in a transaction, and the return value of `queries.update_user_by_username` is assigned directly to `user_in_db.updated_at` to keep the in-memory object consistent with what was persisted [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository::update_user]].

This module serves as the application entry point for the FastAPI service, defining the factory function that assembles the application and immediately invoking it to produce the module-level `app` instance [[target/app/main.py]].

The sole function defined here, `get_application`, is a factory that constructs and fully configures a `FastAPI` application instance, returning it ready for use [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. It begins by retrieving application settings and using them to configure logging [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. A `FastAPI` instance is then created using keyword arguments drawn from those settings [[target/app/main.py::get_application]].

Once the base application is created, `get_application` attaches CORS middleware configured with settings-driven allowed hosts, permitting all HTTP methods and headers and enabling credentials [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. Lifecycle management is handled by registering event handlers for both `"startup"` and `"shutdown"` events: the startup handler is produced by `create_start_app_handler` (receiving both the application and settings), while the shutdown handler is produced by `create_stop_app_handler` (receiving only the application) [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. Error handling is wired up by registering two exception handlers — one for `HTTPException` and one for `RequestValidationError` — each mapped to a dedicated handler function [[target/app/main.py::get_application]]. The API router is then mounted under the prefix defined in settings, completing the assembly before the configured `FastAPI` instance is returned [[target/app/main.py::get_application]].

At module level, `get_application` is called immediately so that the resulting `app` object is available for import by an ASGI server or other consumers [[target/app/main.py]].

`DateTimeModelMixin` is a Pydantic model that serves as a reusable mixin for attaching timestamp fields to other models [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. It inherits from `BaseModel`, making it a first-class Pydantic model whose fields participate in validation and serialization [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. The class is defined in [`target/app/models/common.py`](target/app/models/common.py) across lines 6–15 [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]].

It declares two fields, `created_at` and `updated_at`, both typed as `datetime.datetime` and both defaulting to `None` at the class level [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. Because those defaults are `None` rather than real datetimes, the mixin relies on a validator to supply a live timestamp whenever no explicit value is passed in [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]]. That validator, `default_datetime`, is a class-level method decorated with `@validator("created_at", "updated_at", pre=True)`, so Pydantic invokes it before type coercion for both fields [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]]. It returns the incoming `value` unchanged when one is provided, or falls back to `datetime.datetime.now()` when `value` is falsy [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]]. The practical effect is that any model inheriting from `DateTimeModelMixin` will automatically receive a current timestamp for `created_at` and `updated_at` whenever those fields are omitted [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin::default_datetime]].

This module defines the `Article` domain model, which is the canonical representation of a full article object within the application [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py]].

Through `IDModelMixin` it gains an `id_` field typed `int`, declared with `Field(0, alias="id")` so it serialises under the key `"id"` [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]]. The `RWModel` base provides the shared Pydantic configuration — including camelCase aliasing — that all domain models in the project rely on [[target/app/models/domain/articles.py::Article]].

[`rwmodel.py`](target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py) is a small shared module that defines the base Pydantic model and the two helper functions that configure it [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py]].

`convert_datetime_to_realworld` takes a `datetime.datetime` value, pins it to UTC, and returns an ISO 8601 string with the `+00:00` offset replaced by the compact `Z` suffix, producing the timestamp format expected by most web APIs [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::convert_datetime_to_realworld]]. `convert_field_to_camel_case` takes a snake_case string, keeps the first word lowercase, capitalises the first letter of every subsequent word, and joins them without a separator — converting, for example, `tag_list` to `tagList` [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::convert_field_to_camel_case]].

Both functions feed directly into `RWModel`, the base class that all domain models in this codebase extend [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]]. `RWModel` inherits from Pydantic's `BaseModel` and bundles a nested `Config` that applies three settings to every subclass: `allow_population_by_field_name = True` so that fields can be set using their Python names as well as their aliases; `json_encoders` wired to `convert_datetime_to_realworld` so that `datetime.datetime` values are automatically serialised to the `Z`-suffixed format; and `alias_generator` set to `convert_field_to_camel_case` so that every field is exposed under a camelCase alias without any per-field declaration [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]]. Because the alias generator runs automatically across all fields, any field that requires a *different* alias — such as one that maps to `tagList` from an external API contract — must declare it explicitly with `Field(..., alias="...")` to override the automatic conversion [[target/app/models/domain/rwmodel.py::RWModel]].

`UserInDB` is a Pydantic model that represents a user record as it is stored in the database, extending the base `User` type with identity, timestamp, and credential fields [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. It inherits from three bases: `IDModelMixin`, `DateTimeModelMixin`, and `User` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. From `IDModelMixin` it gains an `id_` field of type `int`, declared with `Field(0, alias="id")` so that it serialises to and from the key `"id"` [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. From `DateTimeModelMixin` it gains `created_at` and `updated_at`, both typed as `datetime.datetime` and defaulting to `None` [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. From `User` it inherits `username: str`, `email: str`, `bio: str` (defaulting to `""`), and `image: Optional[str]` (defaulting to `None`) [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]] [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. On top of those inherited fields, `UserInDB` itself defines two credential fields: `salt: str` (defaulting to `""`) and `hashed_password: str` (defaulting to `""`) [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

The class exposes two methods for managing passwords. `change_password` accepts a plain-text `password: str`, generates a fresh cryptographic salt via `security.generate_salt()`, assigns it to `self.salt`, then concatenates that salt with the password and stores the result of `security.get_password_hash()` in `self.hashed_password`, mutating the instance in place and returning `None` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB::change_password]]. `check_password` accepts a candidate `password: str` and returns a `bool` indicating whether it matches the stored credentials; it prepends `self.salt` to the supplied password and delegates the cryptographic comparison to `security.verify_password`, ensuring the password is never compared in its raw form [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB::check_password]].

This module defines the Pydantic schemas used to validate and serialise article-related data flowing into and out of the API [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]]. It also establishes two module-level constants, `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT` and `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET`, which anchor the default pagination behaviour shared across the schemas [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]].

The central building block is `ArticleForResponse`, which merges the `RWSchema` mixin with the domain `Article` model to produce a fully populated article payload fit for API responses [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]].
