It inherits all core article fields from `Article` — including `slug`, `title`, `description`, `body`, `author`, `favorited`, `favorites_count`, `id_`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` — and adds a single `tags` field exposed under the alias `"tagList"`, overriding the automatic camelCase aliasing that `RWSchema` would otherwise apply [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]].

Two response envelopes wrap that building block. `ArticleInResponse` acts as the top-level wrapper for a single article, exposing one field, `article`, typed as `ArticleForResponse` [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]]. `ListOfArticlesInResponse` covers the collection case, pairing an `articles` list of `ArticleForResponse` items with an `articles_count` integer that records the total number of articles in the result set [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]].

On the request side, `ArticleInCreate` captures the payload for creating a new article, requiring `title`, `description`, and `body` as plain strings while accepting an optional `tags` list (aliased to `"tagList"`, defaulting to empty) [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInCreate]]. `ArticleInUpdate` covers partial edits: all three of its fields — `title`, `description`, and `body` — are `Optional[str]` defaulting to `None`, so a caller may supply any subset of them in a single request [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInUpdate]].

Finally, `ArticlesFilters` handles query-parameter filtering and pagination for article listings [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticlesFilters]]. It inherits directly from `BaseModel` rather than `RWSchema`, and exposes three optional string filters — `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` — alongside `limit` (constrained to at least `1`, defaulting to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT`) and `offset` (constrained to at least `0`, defaulting to `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET`), enabling callers to narrow and page through results in any combination [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticlesFilters]].

This module defines the Pydantic schemas used to validate and serialise comment data at the API boundary [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py]]. All three classes inherit from `RWSchema`, which provides the shared base configuration and camelCase aliasing behaviour common to all schemas in the project [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]].

`CommentInCreate` represents the inbound payload for creating a new comment, exposing a single `body` field of type `str` that carries the comment's text content [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]]. On the response side, `CommentInResponse` wraps a single `Comment` domain object in a `comment` field, providing the schema for an API response that returns one comment [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]]. When multiple comments need to be returned, `ListOfCommentsInResponse` is used instead; it holds a `comments` field typed as `List[Comment]`, serialising the full collection to the caller [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]]. Together, the three schemas cover the complete lifecycle of comment data flowing in and out of the API [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py]].

This module defines the Pydantic schemas used to represent the structured data carried inside a JSON Web Token [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py]]. It contains two models that together cover the two concerns of a JWT payload: token metadata and user identity [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]] [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

`JWTMeta` is a Pydantic `BaseModel` that captures the standard metadata fields of a JWT, namely `exp` (a `datetime` representing the token's expiration time) and `sub` (a `str` representing the token's subject, typically a user identifier) [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]]. `JWTUser` is a second Pydantic `BaseModel` that holds only a single `username` string, representing the authenticated user's identity as extracted from the token payload [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]]. The two models are complementary: `JWTMeta` carries the validity and ownership claims of the token itself, while `JWTUser` carries just enough information to identify who the token belongs to [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]] [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

The module [`target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py) defines the response schema for user profile data, importing `Profile` from the domain layer and wrapping it for API output [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py]]. Its sole class, `ProfileInResponse`, is a Pydantic model that acts as a response envelope for a user profile [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]]. It inherits directly from `BaseModel` and exposes a single field, `profile`, typed as `Profile`, which gives it automatic validation and serialisation of that field at no extra cost [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]].

This module defines the `RWSchema` class, which serves as the shared base for all request/response schema classes in the application [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py]]. `RWSchema` extends `RWModel` and inherits all of its fields, field aliases, and base configuration [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. Its sole addition over the parent is a nested `Config` class that sets `orm_mode = True`, which allows Pydantic to populate model instances directly from ORM objects such as SQLAlchemy rows, rather than requiring plain dictionaries [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. Any schema class that needs both the common behaviour provided by `RWModel` and the ability to read data from ORM results can inherit from `RWSchema` to gain both capabilities at once [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]].

The [`tags.py`](target/app/models/schemas/tags.py) module defines the schema used to represent a collection of tags in API responses [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py]]. It contains a single class, `TagsInList`, which is a Pydantic model inheriting from `BaseModel` [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]]. Its sole responsibility is to wrap a list of tag strings into a structured response object [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]]. It exposes one field, `tags`, typed as `List[str]`, with no default value, meaning the field is required whenever the model is instantiated [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]].

This module defines the Pydantic schemas used to validate and shape user-related request and response data throughout the application [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py]]. It imports from both the domain layer and a shared base schema, then builds a small hierarchy of models that cover the four main user operations: login, registration, update, and response [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py]].

The hierarchy starts with `UserInLogin`, which inherits from `RWSchema` and declares the two fields a user must supply to authenticate: a validated `email` and a plain-string `password` [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInLogin]]. `UserInCreate` extends `UserInLogin` directly, inheriting those two credential fields and adding a required `username` field, making it the complete schema for new account registration [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInCreate]].

For profile edits, `UserInUpdate` stands apart from that inheritance chain; it inherits from `BaseModel` directly and makes all five of its fields — `username`, `email`, `password`, `bio`, and `image` — optional and defaulting to `None`, so a caller can supply any subset when patching a user record [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]]. The `email` field uses `EmailStr` for format validation and `image` uses `HttpUrl` to enforce a valid URL whenever a value is provided [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]].

On the response side, `UserWithToken` extends the domain `User` class, inheriting its `username`, `email`, `bio`, and `image` fields and adding a single required `token: str` field, making it suitable for any response that must carry an authentication token alongside profile data [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserWithToken]]. `UserInResponse` then wraps `UserWithToken` in a single `user` field and inherits from `RWSchema`, ensuring the outgoing payload conforms to the aliasing and serialisation conventions shared across all response schemas in the application [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInResponse]].

The `resources` package is a simple Python package whose sole purpose is to house shared, human-readable content used across the application [[target/app/resources]]. It is marked as a package by an empty initializer file that imposes no logic of its own [[target/app/resources/__init__.py]].

All substantive content lives in a single module, [`strings.py`](target/app/resources/strings.py), which acts as a centralised registry of plain string constants for API error and status messages [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. By concentrating every user-facing text string in one place, the module ensures that wording can be updated without touching any business logic elsewhere in the application [[target/app/resources/strings.py]]. The constants are organised around the main concerns of the API: user and article lookups (covering missing users, missing articles, duplicate articles, and authorisation ownership checks), authentication and registration errors (wrong credentials, taken usernames, taken email addresses), follow and subscription actions (self-follow, self-unfollow, unfollowing a non-followed user, and following an already-followed user), token validation (unsupported authorisation type and unvalidatable payload), favouriting actions (already favourited and not yet favourited), comment existence, and a general authentication-required notice [[target/app/resources/strings.py]].

`target/app/services/articles.py` is a small service module that collects article-related business logic — existence checks, slug generation, and ownership authorization — in one place [[target/app/services/articles.py]].

`check_article_exists` is an asynchronous helper that determines whether an article identified by a given slug is present in the data store [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]]. It accepts an `ArticlesRepository` instance and a `slug` string, delegates the actual lookup to `articles_repo.get_article_by_slug`, and returns `False` if `EntityDoesNotExist` is raised or `True` if the call succeeds [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]].

`get_slug_for_article` is a thin utility that converts a plain article title into a URL-friendly slug by delegating entirely to a `slugify` call and returning the result directly [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]]. It performs no additional logic of its own [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]].

`check_user_can_modify_article` is an authorization helper that decides whether a given user may modify an article by comparing `article.author.username` with `user.username`, returning `True` when they match and `False` otherwise [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]]. Ownership is determined solely by that username equality check, with no external dependencies beyond its two arguments [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]].

Together the three functions form a lightweight service layer: `get_slug_for_article` produces the slug used to identify an article, `check_article_exists` verifies that a slug resolves to a real record, and `check_user_can_modify_article` enforces that only the article's author may alter it [[target/app/services/articles.py]].

[`target/app/services/authentication.py`](target/app/services/authentication.py) is a small service module that provides uniqueness checks for user credentials during registration [[target/app/services/authentication.py]]. It contains two asynchronous functions, `check_username_is_taken` and `check_email_is_taken`, both of which follow the same pattern: they accept a `UsersRepository` instance and a credential string, delegate a lookup to the repository, and return a `bool` indicating whether the credential is already in use [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]].

[`check_username_is_taken`](target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken) calls `repo.get_user_by_username` with the provided username and returns `True` if the call succeeds, meaning a matching user already exists [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]]. If the repository raises `EntityDoesNotExist` — signalling that no such user was found — the function catches the exception and returns `False` instead [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]].

[`check_email_is_taken`](target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken) mirrors this behaviour for email addresses, delegating to `repo.get_user_by_email` and applying the same exception-as-signal convention: a raised `EntityDoesNotExist` means the email is unclaimed and yields `False`, while a successful lookup yields `True` [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]]. Both functions rely entirely on the repository layer for data access and use `EntityDoesNotExist` as their sole control-flow signal, keeping the service layer free of direct database concerns [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]].

This module serves as the service layer for comment-related authorization logic, providing a single utility for determining whether a user has the right to modify a specific comment [[target/app/services/comments.py]]. It defines one function, [`check_user_can_modify_comment()`](target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment), which accepts a `Comment` and a `User` and returns a `bool` indicating whether the given user owns the given comment [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]]. The check is performed by comparing the username stored on the comment's author against the username of the supplied user, returning `True` on a match and `False` otherwise [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]]. The function is intentionally minimal: it carries no decorators, raises no exceptions, and introduces no side effects, making it a pure ownership predicate that higher-level request handlers can call before allowing a mutation to proceed [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]].

[`target/app/services/jwt.py`](target/app/services/jwt.py) is responsible for creating and verifying JSON Web Tokens used to authenticate users in the application [[target/app/services/jwt.py]]. It establishes three module-level constants that govern all tokens produced here: `JWT_SUBJECT` fixes the token's `sub` claim to `"access"`, `ALGORITHM` sets the signing algorithm to `HS256`, and `ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES` defines a default lifetime of one week [[target/app/services/jwt.py]].

The lowest-level building block is [`create_jwt_token()`](target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token), a keyword-only function that accepts an arbitrary claims dictionary, a secret key, and an expiry duration, and returns a signed JWT string [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]]. It copies the caller's claims dictionary to avoid mutation, merges in a `JWTMeta` object carrying the computed expiry timestamp and the fixed subject, and passes the combined payload to `jwt.encode` along with the secret key and the module-level `ALGORITHM` constant [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]].

[`create_access_token_for_user()`](target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user) is the higher-level convenience wrapper intended for normal application use [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]]. It accepts a `User` domain object and a secret key, packages the user's username into a `JWTUser` payload, and delegates to `create_jwt_token` with an expiry duration derived from the module-level `ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES` constant [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]].

The complementary function [`get_username_from_token()`](target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token) reverses the process: it decodes a JWT string using the same secret key and algorithm, unpacks the result into a `JWTUser` model, and returns the embedded username [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]]. Two distinct error paths are handled — a `jwt.PyJWTError` (covering invalid signatures or expired tokens) is re-raised as a `ValueError` with the message `"unable to decode JWT token"`, while a `ValidationError` (covering a token whose payload does not match the expected `JWTUser` shape) is re-raised as a `ValueError` with the message `"malformed payload in token"`, with the original exception chained in both cases to preserve the root cause [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]].

This module is a focused security utility layer responsible for password hashing and verification [[target/app/services/security.py]]. It configures a shared `pwd_context` using `passlib`'s `CryptContext` with bcrypt as the hashing scheme, and all three of its functions delegate their core cryptographic work to either that context or the `bcrypt` library directly [[target/app/services/security.py]].

`generate_salt` produces a fresh cryptographic salt as a plain UTF-8 string by calling `bcrypt.gensalt()` and decoding the resulting bytes [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]]. It takes no arguments and has no side effects, making it a simple, self-contained utility [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]].

`get_password_hash` accepts a plain-text password string and returns its hashed form by forwarding the work entirely to `pwd_context.hash` [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]]. It contains no branching logic and raises no exceptions of its own, acting as a thin wrapper around the configured context [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]].

`verify_password` takes a plain-text password and a stored hash, and returns a boolean indicating whether they match, delegating entirely to `pwd_context.verify` for the comparison [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]]. Like its siblings, it introduces no additional logic or exception handling beyond what the underlying context provides [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]].

Together, the three functions form a cohesive, thin abstraction over `bcrypt` and `passlib`, keeping all cryptographic policy in one place through the shared `pwd_context` [[target/app/services/security.py]].

This module is the central authentication layer for the FastAPI application, responsible for extracting JWT bearer tokens from incoming HTTP requests, validating them, and resolving the authenticated user as a dependency [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]].

The foundation is [`RWAPIKeyHeader`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader), a custom subclass of FastAPI's `APIKeyHeader` that overrides the async `__call__` method to intercept any `StarletteHTTPException` raised when the `Authorization` header is missing, re-raising it as a project-local `HTTPException` with a standardised authentication-required message [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]]. This ensures all authentication failures surface with a consistent error shape across the application [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::RWAPIKeyHeader]].

On top of that, [`_get_authorization_header`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header) uses `RWAPIKeyHeader` as a `Security` dependency to retrieve the raw header string, then splits it into a prefix and a token, raising a `403 Forbidden` exception if the value cannot be split or if the prefix does not match the configured `jwt_token_prefix` [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header]]. Its counterpart, [`_get_authorization_header_optional`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional), wraps the same logic but supplies `auto_error=False` to `RWAPIKeyHeader` so that a missing header returns an empty string rather than an error, making it safe for optional-auth endpoints [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_optional]]. The factory function [`_get_authorization_header_retriever`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever) selects between these two callables based on a `required` boolean flag, returning `_get_authorization_header` when authentication is mandatory and `_get_authorization_header_optional` when it is not [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_authorization_header_retriever]].

With a validated token in hand, [`_get_current_user`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user) decodes the JWT via `jwt.get_username_from_token`, raising `403 Forbidden` on a malformed payload, and then looks up the identified username in the database through a `UsersRepository`; if no matching record exists an `EntityDoesNotExist` exception is caught and the same `403 Forbidden` response is returned, preventing username enumeration [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user]]. Its sibling, [`_get_current_user_optional`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional), delegates to `_get_current_user` when a token is present and returns `None` when no credentials are supplied, yielding an `Optional[User]` return type that covers both authenticated and anonymous callers [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::_get_current_user_optional]].

The public surface of the module is the factory function [`get_current_user_authorizer`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer), which route handlers call with a `required` keyword argument to obtain either `_get_current_user` or `_get_current_user_optional` as their FastAPI dependency, giving each endpoint a single, declarative way to express whether an unauthenticated request should be rejected or tolerated [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]].

The `errors` package is the centralized error-handling layer for the FastAPI application, grouping the components responsible for converting exceptions into consistent JSON responses [[target/app/api/errors]]. Its `__init__.py` is an empty initializer that simply marks the directory as a Python package [[target/app/api/errors/__init__.py]].

The package contains two handler modules. The first, `http_error.py`, defines the asynchronous `http_error_handler` function, which intercepts any raised `HTTPException` and wraps it in a JSON response whose body carries a single `"errors"` key mapped to a list containing `exc.detail`, with the HTTP status code taken directly from `exc.status_code` [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py::http_error_handler]]. This ensures that every HTTP error reaching the client arrives in a uniform envelope rather than as a raw or framework-default response [[target/app/api/errors/http_error.py]].

The second module, `validation_error.py`, handles the narrower case of validation failures through its `http422_error_handler` function, which accepts either a `RequestValidationError` or a `ValidationError` so that both FastAPI-level and Pydantic-level failures are covered [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]]. It calls `exc.errors()` to extract the structured list of problems and returns a `JSONResponse` with status code `HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY`, again placing the error list under an `"errors"` key to match the envelope established by the HTTP error handler [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py::http422_error_handler]]. Additionally, the module rewrites the `"properties"` entry of `validation_error_response_definition` at import time so that the auto-generated OpenAPI documentation stays consistent with the actual response shape the handler produces [[target/app/api/errors/validation_error.py]].

The `articles` package is the self-contained routing layer that handles every HTTP endpoint related to articles in the application [[target/app/api/routes/articles]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py) contains no definitions but marks the directory as an importable Python package, making the submodules available to the rest of the routing hierarchy [[target/app/api/routes/articles/__init__.py]].

The package is divided into three substantive modules whose responsibilities are kept distinct and then unified in one place [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]]. [`api.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py) acts as the assembly point: it creates a single `APIRouter` and mounts the two sub-routers from `articles_common` and `articles_resource` under the `/articles` URL prefix, so the broader application only needs to register this one combined router [[target/app/api/routes/articles/api.py]].

[`articles_resource.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py) owns the five core CRUD operations for articles [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py]]. It handles listing articles with optional tag, author, favourited, limit, and offset filters — with authentication being optional so unauthenticated callers can still browse — as well as creating, retrieving, updating, and deleting individual articles identified by their URL slug [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::list_articles]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::create_new_article]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]]. Slug-based article resolution is handled by a shared dependency before the handler body runs, so retrieval, update, and delete handlers all receive the already-resolved article object [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::retrieve_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]]. The update and delete handlers additionally enforce an authorisation check through a route-level `check_article_modification_permissions` dependency declared in their decorators, ensuring ownership is verified before any mutation occurs [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]].

[`articles_common.py`](target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py) covers the two remaining cross-cutting concerns: the authenticated user's personalised article feed and the favouriting system [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]]. The `GET /feed` handler returns a paginated list of articles scoped to the current user, with `limit` and `offset` bounds validated by FastAPI's `Query` [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::get_articles_for_user_feed]]. The `POST /{slug}/favorite` and `DELETE /{slug}/favorite` handlers are mirror images of each other: the first persists a favourite relationship and returns the article with `favorited` set to `True` and `favorites_count` incremented in memory, while the second removes the relationship and decrements the count, and both raise an HTTP 400 error if the requested state already matches the current one [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]]. All three handlers in this module share the same dependency injection pattern — authentication via `get_current_user_authorizer()` and database access via `get_repository(ArticlesRepository)` — making the module a cohesive set of endpoints built on a common foundation [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py]].

[`target/app/core/logging.py`](target/app/core/logging.py) is a small bridge module whose sole purpose is to route all standard-library log records into Loguru for unified log handling [[target/app/core/logging.py]]. It defines exactly one class, [`InterceptHandler`](target/app/core/logging.py), which is a concrete subclass of `logging.Handler` and carries no Pydantic model machinery of its own [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

`InterceptHandler` expresses all of its behaviour through a single overridden method, `emit`, which accepts a `logging.LogRecord` and returns `None`, satisfying the abstract contract that `logging.Handler` requires [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. When a record arrives, `emit` first maps the record's level name to a Loguru-native level via `logger.level`; if Loguru does not recognise the name and raises a `ValueError`, it falls back to the raw integer level number as a string [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. It then walks the call stack upward past any frames whose source file belongs to the `logging` module itself, so that Loguru can attribute the event to the true call site rather than an internal logging frame [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]]. With the correct stack depth in hand, it calls `logger.opt` with that depth and the record's `exc_info`, then forwards the event to Loguru via `.log` using the resolved level and the message returned by `record.getMessage` [[target/app/core/logging.py::InterceptHandler]].

The [`app.py`](target/app/core/settings/app.py) module defines the primary runtime configuration for the application, housing a single class that consolidates every setting the web server, database, authentication, and logging subsystems require [[target/app/core/settings/app.py]].

[`AppSettings`](target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings) is a Pydantic model that extends `BaseAppSettings` to add all of those runtime settings in one place [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. Its fields are organised around four concerns. For the FastAPI layer it declares `debug`, `docs_url`, `openapi_prefix`, `openapi_url`, `redoc_url`, `title`, and `version`, all carrying sensible defaults so the server can start without explicit overrides [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For the database it requires a `database_url` typed as `PostgresDsn` — meaning the application cannot start without it — and accepts `max_connection_count` and `min_connection_count`, both defaulting to `10` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For authentication it requires a `secret_key` of type `SecretStr` alongside `api_prefix`, `jwt_token_prefix`, and `allowed_hosts` [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. For logging it holds `logging_level` and a two-element `loggers` tuple naming the Uvicorn loggers that should be intercepted [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. An inner `Config` class enables `validate_assignment`, so Pydantic enforces type constraints on any field that is updated after the object is constructed, not only at initialisation time [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

The class exposes two behaviours that the rest of the application consume directly. The `fastapi_kwargs` read-only property packages the seven FastAPI-relevant fields into a plain dictionary that can be unpacked straight into the FastAPI constructor, keeping instantiation boilerplate out of the application factory [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The `configure_logging` method wires the root logger and each logger named in `self.loggers` to Loguru's `InterceptHandler`, then adds a Loguru sink writing to `sys.stderr` at `self.logging_level`, so every intercepted log record is ultimately funnelled through a single handler [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

This module defines the table reference layer used to construct type-annotated pypika queries against the application's PostgreSQL database [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

The foundation is `Parameter`, a thin subclass of pypika's `CommonParameter` that overrides placeholder formatting to produce asyncpg-style positional parameters — `$1`, `$2`, and so on — instead of the default style, making it compatible with the asyncpg driver used elsewhere in the application [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Parameter]].

Above that sits `TypedTable`, a subclass of pypika's `Table` that introduces a class-level `__table__` attribute [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]]. When a subclass sets `__table__`, the constructor resolves the database table name from it automatically, falling back to the class's own `__name__` if `__table__` is absent; this lets each subclass act as a self-describing table reference without any construction-time arguments [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]].

All five concrete table classes inherit from `TypedTable` and carry typed field annotations that mirror their respective database columns. `Users` maps to the `"users"` table and declares `id` and `username` [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Users]]. `Articles` maps to `"articles"` and declares eight fields — `id`, `slug`, `title`, `description`, `body`, `author_id`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Articles]]. `Tags` maps to `"tags"` with a single `tag` string column [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Tags]]. `ArticlesToTags` maps to `"articles_to_tags"` and carries `article_id` and `tag`, representing the join between articles and their tags [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::ArticlesToTags]]. `Favorites` maps to `"favorites"` with `article_id` and `user_id`, linking a user to a favorited article [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Favorites]].

The module closes by instantiating each table class once — `users`, `articles`, `tags`, `articles_to_tags`, and `favorites` — producing the shared singleton table references that query-building code imports directly [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

This module is the data-access layer for all article-related database operations in the application [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py]]. It defines a single class, `ArticlesRepository`, which inherits from `BaseRepository` and centralises every interaction with the articles table — creation, retrieval, filtering, updating, deletion, and favourites management [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

The class is initialised with an asyncpg `Connection` object that is forwarded to the parent class for shared infrastructure, while two collaborating repositories — `ProfilesRepository` and `TagsRepository` — are instantiated on the same connection and stored as `self._profiles_repo` and `self._tags_repo` [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. This design means the class carries no independently declared data fields beyond that inherited connection and the two sub-repository references [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

On the write side, `create_article` persists a new article row inside a database transaction, optionally upserts any supplied tags through `_tags_repo`, attaches them to the article via the private `_link_article_with_tags` helper, and then hydrates a full `Article` domain object from the returned raw row [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `update_article` deep-copies the existing `Article`, applies whichever optional field overrides were provided among `slug`, `title`, `body`, and `description`, runs the update inside a transaction, and returns the copy with `updated_at` set to the timestamp the database echoes back [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `delete_article` wraps row removal in a transaction, keying the lookup on the article's slug and author username [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `add_article_into_favorites` and `remove_article_from_favorites` each delegate directly to a named query, translating the `Article` and `User` domain objects into the slug and username identifiers the query layer requires [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

On the read side, `get_article_by_slug` fetches a single raw row by slug and raises `EntityDoesNotExist` when none is found, otherwise forwarding the row to the private assembly helper [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `filter_articles` dynamically builds a pypika query, conditionally joining `articles_to_tags`, `users`, and `favorites` when the `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` arguments are respectively supplied, and appends `limit` and `offset` as positional asyncpg parameters before converting each result row into an `Article` [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `get_articles_for_user_feed` retrieves articles authored by users that the requesting user follows, paginating with `limit` and `offset` and hydrating each row in the same manner [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `get_tags_for_article_by_slug` returns a plain list of tag strings for a given slug, while `get_favorites_count_for_article_by_slug` returns the integer favourite count, and `is_article_favorited_by_user` returns a boolean indicating whether a specific user has favourited a specific article [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

Two private helpers underpin all of the above. `_get_article_from_db_record` is the central assembly point: it reads scalar fields from the raw database `Record` and then issues additional async calls to fetch the author's profile with follow-state, the article's tags, the favourites count, and — only when a `requested_user` is present — the per-user favourited flag, defaulting to `False` for unauthenticated callers [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. `_link_article_with_tags` constructs a list of `{slug, tag}` dictionaries and forwards it to the named query `add_tags_to_article`, serving exclusively as an internal helper for write paths that need to associate tags with an article [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].

This module defines the shared foundation for all database repository classes in the application [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py]]. It contains a single class, `BaseRepository`, which acts as the root of the repository hierarchy without declaring any base classes of its own [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]].

`BaseRepository` is a plain Python class whose constructor accepts a single `conn` parameter of type `Connection` and stores it as the private instance attribute `_conn`, with no additional logic or side effects [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. This stored connection is the live database connection that all methods in the class hierarchy rely on [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]].

Public access to that connection is provided through the read-only `connection` property, decorated with `@property`, which returns `_conn` as a `Connection` instance [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]]. Because no setter is defined, the connection cannot be reassigned after construction, giving subclasses and callers a controlled, uniform interface to the injected connection [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py::BaseRepository]].

This module provides the data-access layer for all comment-related persistence operations in the application, defining a single class that mediates between the database and the comment domain model [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py]].

`CommentsRepository` is the sole class defined here; it inherits from `BaseRepository` and is responsible for creating, retrieving, and deleting comments [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. Its constructor accepts a `Connection`, forwards it to the parent class to initialise shared connection handling, and also creates an internal `ProfilesRepository` instance stored as `self._profiles_repo` — reflecting a deliberate design dependency, since fully hydrating a comment requires resolving its author's profile [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

The class exposes four public async methods. `get_comment_by_id` fetches a single comment scoped to a specific article by numeric ID, raising `EntityDoesNotExist` with a descriptive message when no matching row is found rather than returning `None` [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. `get_comments_for_article` retrieves all comments for a given article's slug and returns them as a list of `Comment` domain objects, accepting an optional requesting user so that each author's follow state can be resolved correctly [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. `create_comment_for_article` persists a new comment from a body string, an `Article`, and an authoring `User`, then returns the fully hydrated `Comment` [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. `delete_comment` is a thin async wrapper that delegates entirely to the underlying query, accepting a `Comment` instance and returning nothing [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

All four public methods depend on the private helper `_get_comment_from_db_record`, which assembles a `Comment` domain object from a raw database `Record` by reading the `id`, `body`, `created_at`, and `updated_at` columns directly from the row and awaiting `self._profiles_repo.get_profile_by_username` to resolve the author before construction [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]]. The optional `requested_user` is forwarded through this helper to the profile lookup so that follow state is always determined relative to the currently authenticated user [[target/app/db/repositories/comments.py::CommentsRepository]].

This module defines the `ProfilesRepository` class and a `UserLike` type alias, forming the dedicated data-access layer for user profiles and follower relationships [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py]]. The `UserLike` alias unions `User` and `Profile`, allowing methods throughout the file to accept either domain type interchangeably [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py]].

`ProfilesRepository` inherits from `BaseRepository` and serves as the single point of access for all profile reads and follow-graph mutations in the database layer [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. Its constructor takes an `asyncpg` `Connection`, passes it up to the parent class, and also constructs an internal `UsersRepository` instance stored as `self._users_repo`, so that user-level lookups are available without duplicating connection management [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

The `get_profile_by_username` method ties the class together: it delegates the raw user lookup to `self._users_repo`, assembles a `Profile` from the returned record's `username`, `bio`, and `image` fields, and — when a `requested_user` is supplied — populates the `following` field by calling `is_user_following_for_another_user` on the same repository instance [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. The `is_user_following_for_another_user` method handles that follow-status check by forwarding `requested_user.username` as the follower and `target_user.username` as the followee to a named SQL query, then returning the boolean `"is_following"` value from its result [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

Mutating the follow graph is handled by the symmetric pair `add_user_into_followers` and `remove_user_from_followers`, both of which accept `target_user` and `requested_user` as keyword-only `UserLike` arguments [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. `add_user_into_followers` opens a database transaction and calls the `subscribe_user_to_another` query to record the relationship, while `remove_user_from_followers` opens a transaction and calls `unsubscribe_user_from_another` to delete it, both returning `None` [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]].

This module defines the tag-related database access layer for the application, containing a single repository class that handles all tag persistence concerns [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py]].

`TagsRepository` inherits from `BaseRepository` and is responsible for managing tag records in the database [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. It declares no fields of its own, relying entirely on the connection object provided by its base class, which it passes through to every query call [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. The class exposes two asynchronous methods that together cover the read and write operations needed for tags [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. The first, `get_all_tags`, retrieves every stored tag from the database and returns them as a flat `List[str]` by extracting the first column from each result row [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. The second, `create_tags_that_dont_exist`, accepts a keyword-only `tags` argument — a sequence of strings — and persists any tags not yet present in the database by delegating to the shared `queries` object with a list of `{"tag": tag}` dictionaries, one per input entry, returning `None` on completion [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]]. Both methods immediately await their respective query calls, participating in the async I/O model used throughout the repository layer [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]].

This module is the data-access layer for all user-related database operations in the application [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py]]. It defines a single class, `UsersRepository`, which inherits from `BaseRepository` and relies on the shared `connection` attribute that parent class supplies to every method [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

`UsersRepository` exposes four asynchronous methods that together cover the full lifecycle of a user record [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. `get_user_by_email` and `get_user_by_username` are lookup methods that each delegate to the `queries` layer, return a `UserInDB` instance on success, and raise `EntityDoesNotExist` with a descriptive message when no matching row is found [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. The two methods follow the same structural pattern, differing only in which field — email or username — drives the query [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

`create_user` accepts a `username`, `email`, and `password`, constructs a transient `UserInDB` object, hashes the password before any database interaction occurs, and inserts the record inside an atomic transaction [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. It returns the result of merging the freshly inserted row — including any server-generated values such as an auto-assigned id or timestamps — back onto the in-memory model [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

`update_user` takes an existing `User` object together with five optional keyword arguments — `username`, `email`, `password`, `bio`, and `image` — and applies selective updates to the stored record [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. It first fetches the current database state by calling `get_user_by_username` internally, then merges each provided field using a short-circuit `or` so that absent arguments leave stored values unchanged, and derives fresh salt and hash values if a new password is supplied [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]]. The entire write is wrapped in a transaction, and the timestamp returned by the underlying query is assigned directly to the in-memory object so it remains consistent with what was persisted [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

[`target/app/models/common.py`](target/app/models/common.py) is a shared module that provides two lightweight Pydantic mixins intended to be composed into domain models throughout the application [[target/app/models/common.py]].

`DateTimeModelMixin` attaches `created_at` and `updated_at` timestamp fields to any model that inherits from it [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. Both fields are typed as `datetime.datetime` and default to `None` at the class level, with a pre-validation hook supplying a live `datetime.datetime.now()` call whenever a value is not explicitly provided [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]]. This means inheriting models receive accurate creation and update timestamps automatically without any extra wiring at the call site [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]].

`IDModelMixin` adds a single integer identity field to models that need one [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]]. The field is declared as `id_` in Python to avoid shadowing the built-in `id`, but is aliased to `"id"` so that it serialises and deserialises under the conventional key expected by API consumers and database rows [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]]. The default value of `0` means the field is always present and safe to read even before a real database-assigned identifier has been attached [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]].

The two mixins are independent of each other and can be combined freely; a domain model that needs both a stable identity and automatic timestamps simply inherits from both [[target/app/models/common.py::DateTimeModelMixin]] [[target/app/models/common.py::IDModelMixin]].

This module defines the user domain models for the application, providing both a lightweight representation for in-memory use and a richer record type for database persistence [[target/app/models/domain/users.py]].

`User` is the base domain model, inheriting from `RWModel` and declaring four fields: the required `username` and `email` strings, a `bio` string that defaults to an empty string, and an optional `image` string that defaults to `None` [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]]. It captures only the data needed to describe a user at the application layer, without any identity or credential information [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::User]].

`UserInDB` extends `User` by also inheriting from `IDModelMixin` and `DateTimeModelMixin`, adding an integer `id_` field (aliased to `"id"` for serialisation), `created_at` and `updated_at` datetime fields, and two credential fields — `salt` and `hashed_password` — both defaulting to empty strings [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]. This makes `UserInDB` the complete picture of a stored user row, combining profile data with the identity and timestamp information managed by the mixins [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

The two password methods on `UserInDB` work in tandem: `change_password` generates a fresh salt, concatenates it with the supplied plain-text password, hashes the result, and mutates the instance's `salt` and `hashed_password` fields in place [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]]; `check_password` then mirrors that process at verification time by prepending the stored salt to the candidate password before delegating the comparison to `security.verify_password`, ensuring the raw password is never compared directly [[target/app/models/domain/users.py::UserInDB]].

The `schemas` package is the API boundary layer for the application, grouping all Pydantic models that validate incoming requests and serialise outgoing responses [[target/app/models/schemas]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/models/schemas/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, doing nothing beyond making the directory a proper Python package so that other modules can import from it [[target/app/models/schemas/__init__.py]].

The foundation for nearly every schema in the package is `RWSchema`, defined in [`rwschema.py`](target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py) [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py]]. It extends `RWModel` and adds a `Config` with `orm_mode = True`, which lets Pydantic populate schema instances directly from ORM row objects rather than requiring plain dictionaries [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]]. Any schema that needs both the shared aliasing behaviour of `RWModel` and the ability to read ORM results inherits from `RWSchema` [[target/app/models/schemas/rwschema.py::RWSchema]].

User-facing schemas live in [`users.py`](target/app/models/schemas/users.py) [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py]]. `UserInLogin` captures the email and password required to authenticate, and `UserInCreate` extends it with a `username` field to cover new account registration [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInLogin]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInCreate]]. For partial profile edits, `UserInUpdate` inherits directly from `BaseModel` and makes all five of its fields optional, including `EmailStr`-validated email and `HttpUrl`-validated image [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInUpdate]]. On the response side, `UserWithToken` appends a `token` field to the domain `User`, and `UserInResponse` wraps it in a single `user` envelope that inherits from `RWSchema` for consistent serialisation [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserWithToken]] [[target/app/models/schemas/users.py::UserInResponse]].

JWT-related data is handled separately in [`jwt.py`](target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py) [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py]]. `JWTMeta` holds the standard `exp` and `sub` claims that govern a token's validity and ownership, while `JWTUser` holds only the `username` needed to identify the authenticated party [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTMeta]] [[target/app/models/schemas/jwt.py::JWTUser]].

Article schemas are defined in [`articles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/articles.py), which also declares the module-level pagination constants `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_LIMIT` and `DEFAULT_ARTICLES_OFFSET` [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py]]. `ArticleForResponse` merges `RWSchema` with the domain `Article` model, carrying all core article fields and exposing tags under the explicit alias `"tagList"` [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleForResponse]]. It is then wrapped by `ArticleInResponse` for single-article responses and by `ListOfArticlesInResponse`, which pairs the collection with an `articles_count` total, for list responses [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ListOfArticlesInResponse]]. Inbound article data is validated by `ArticleInCreate`, which requires `title`, `description`, and `body`, and by `ArticleInUpdate`, which makes all three optional for partial edits [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticleInUpdate]]. Filtering and pagination of article listings is handled by `ArticlesFilters`, a `BaseModel` subclass that exposes optional `tag`, `author`, and `favorited` filters alongside bounded `limit` and `offset` fields [[target/app/models/schemas/articles.py::ArticlesFilters]].

Comment schemas in [`comments.py`](target/app/models/schemas/comments.py) follow the same pattern [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py]]. `CommentInCreate` carries the single `body` string for a new comment, `CommentInResponse` wraps one domain `Comment` object, and `ListOfCommentsInResponse` wraps a full list, all three inheriting from `RWSchema` [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInCreate]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::CommentInResponse]] [[target/app/models/schemas/comments.py::ListOfCommentsInResponse]].

Profile and tag responses are each handled by a single, focused schema. `ProfileInResponse` in [`profiles.py`](target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py) inherits from `BaseModel` and wraps the domain `Profile` in a `profile` field [[target/app/models/schemas/profiles.py::ProfileInResponse]]. `TagsInList` in [`tags.py`](target/app/models/schemas/tags.py) likewise inherits from `BaseModel` and exposes a required `tags` field typed as `List[str]`, providing a structured envelope for tag collections returned by the API [[target/app/models/schemas/tags.py::TagsInList]].

The `services` package is the application's business-logic layer, grouping credential validation, article and comment authorization, token management, and password security into focused modules [[target/app/services]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/services/__init__.py) is intentionally empty, existing solely to make the directory importable as a Python package and defining no functions, classes, or imports of its own [[target/app/services/__init__.py]].

Registration-time uniqueness checks live in [`authentication.py`](target/app/services/authentication.py), which exposes two async functions — `check_username_is_taken` and `check_email_is_taken` — each delegating a repository lookup and translating a caught `EntityDoesNotExist` exception into a `False` return value [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_username_is_taken]] [[target/app/services/authentication.py::check_email_is_taken]]. By relying entirely on the repository layer and using the exception as their only control-flow signal, these functions keep the service layer free of direct database concerns [[target/app/services/authentication.py]].

Article-related logic is collected in [`articles.py`](target/app/services/articles.py), which provides three cooperating helpers [[target/app/services/articles.py]]. `get_slug_for_article` converts a title into a URL-friendly slug via a `slugify` call, `check_article_exists` asynchronously verifies that the slug resolves to a real record by delegating to `ArticlesRepository.get_article_by_slug` and catching `EntityDoesNotExist`, and `check_user_can_modify_article` enforces ownership by comparing the article author's username against the requesting user's username [[target/app/services/articles.py::get_slug_for_article]] [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_article_exists]] [[target/app/services/articles.py::check_user_can_modify_article]].

Comment ownership follows the same pattern in [`comments.py`](target/app/services/comments.py), where `check_user_can_modify_comment` accepts a `Comment` and a `User`, compares usernames, and returns a plain boolean with no side effects, exceptions, or external dependencies [[target/app/services/comments.py::check_user_can_modify_comment]].

JWT lifecycle is handled by [`jwt.py`](target/app/services/jwt.py), which anchors all tokens to the `"access"` subject, the `HS256` algorithm, and a one-week default lifetime [[target/app/services/jwt.py]]. The low-level `create_jwt_token` merges caller-supplied claims with computed expiry metadata before calling `jwt.encode`, while the higher-level `create_access_token_for_user` wraps it for ordinary application use by packaging a `User` object's username into the payload [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_jwt_token]] [[target/app/services/jwt.py::create_access_token_for_user]]. The complementary `get_username_from_token` decodes a token and surfaces two distinct failure modes — an invalid or expired token raises a `ValueError` with the message `"unable to decode JWT token"`, and a structurally malformed payload raises a `ValueError` with the message `"malformed payload in token"` — in both cases chaining the original exception [[target/app/services/jwt.py::get_username_from_token]].

Password operations are concentrated in [`security.py`](target/app/services/security.py), which configures a single shared `CryptContext` using bcrypt and exposes three thin wrappers around it [[target/app/services/security.py]]. `generate_salt` calls `bcrypt.gensalt()` and decodes the result to a UTF-8 string, `get_password_hash` forwards a plain-text password to `pwd_context.hash`, and `verify_password` delegates comparison of a password and a stored hash to `pwd_context.verify`, keeping all cryptographic policy in one place [[target/app/services/security.py::generate_salt]] [[target/app/services/security.py::get_password_hash]] [[target/app/services/security.py::verify_password]].

The `dependencies` package is the shared dependency-injection layer for the FastAPI application, grouping all reusable `Depends`-based functions that route handlers across the API rely on for authentication, database access, and resource resolution [[target/app/api/dependencies]]. Its `__init__.py` contains no definitions of its own, but its presence makes all the components defined in the submodules importable as a cohesive unit [[target/app/api/dependencies/__init__.py]].

Database connectivity is provided by [`database.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/database.py), which exposes a three-step chain: the application-level asyncpg pool is read from `request.app.state.pool`, a single connection is acquired from that pool and automatically released after the request scope exits, and the public factory `get_repository` wraps both steps so that any route handler can declare a specific repository class through a single `Depends(get_repository(SomeRepository))` expression [[target/app/api/dependencies/database.py]].

Authentication is centralised in [`authentication.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py), which extracts JWT bearer tokens from the `Authorization` header, validates their prefix and payload, and resolves the caller to a `User` record from the database [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py]]. The public entry point is `get_current_user_authorizer`, a factory that route handlers call with a `required` flag to obtain either a strict dependency that rejects unauthenticated requests with `403 Forbidden` or an optional one that returns `None` for anonymous callers, giving each endpoint a single declarative way to express its authentication requirement [[target/app/api/dependencies/authentication.py::get_current_user_authorizer]].

Resource resolution is split across three domain-specific modules. [`articles.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py) supplies `get_articles_filters` for packaging query-string filter parameters into a typed `ArticlesFilters` object, `get_article_by_slug_from_path` for resolving a URL slug into an `Article` (converting a missing record into a `404 Not Found` HTTP response), and `check_article_modification_permissions` for enforcing author-only write access by raising `403 Forbidden` when the authenticated user is not the article's author [[target/app/api/dependencies/articles.py]]. [`comments.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py) mirrors this pattern with `get_comment_by_id_from_path`, which resolves a comment scoped to its parent article and converts `EntityDoesNotExist` into a `404`, and `check_comment_modification_permissions`, which builds on top of that resolver to enforce write-access control, forming a dependency chain so that any route requiring modification permissions automatically inherits comment resolution and 404 handling [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::check_comment_modification_permissions]] [[target/app/api/dependencies/comments.py::get_comment_by_id_from_path]]. [`profiles.py`](target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py) follows the same approach with its single export `get_profile_by_username_from_path`, which resolves a username from the URL path into a `Profile` object, forwarding the optional requesting user to the repository so that viewer-relative state such as follow relationships is included in the result, and translating a missing profile into a `404 Not Found` response [[target/app/api/dependencies/profiles.py::get_profile_by_username_from_path]].

Taken together, the package ensures that authentication, connection management, and per-resource lookup and authorisation logic are defined once and composed declaratively, keeping individual route handlers free of repetitive boilerplate [[target/app/api/dependencies]].

The `routes` package is the complete HTTP routing layer of the application, grouping every endpoint the API exposes into focused submodules that are then unified in one place [[target/app/api/routes]]. Its [`__init__.py`](target/app/api/routes/__init__.py) contains no definitions of its own and exists solely to make the directory importable as a Python package [[target/app/api/routes/__init__.py]].

The assembly point for the entire surface is [`api.py`](target/app/api/routes/api.py), which creates a root `APIRouter` and registers six sub-routers onto it, each bound to a URL prefix and a tag for the generated OpenAPI schema [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. Authentication routes are mounted under `/users`, user-management routes under `/user`, and profile routes under `/profiles`; article routes carry no additional prefix, comment routes nest under `/articles/{slug}/comments`, and tag routes sit under `/tags` [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]]. The articles sub-router is drawn from a nested package rather than a flat sibling module, while every other sub-router is imported directly from its own file in this directory [[target/app/api/routes/api.py]].

Authentication is handled by [`authentication.py`](target/app/api/routes/authentication.py), which exposes two POST endpoints for login and registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py]]. The login handler verifies credentials against the `UsersRepository`, raises HTTP 400 on an unknown email or wrong password, and on success returns a `UserInResponse` wrapping a freshly minted JWT [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]]. The registration handler first checks that neither the requested username nor email is already taken, then creates the record and immediately issues a token so the caller is authenticated from the moment of registration [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]]. Both handlers accept `UsersRepository` and `AppSettings` via dependency injection and produce the same `UserInResponse` containing a `UserWithToken` [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::login]] [[target/app/api/routes/authentication.py::register]].

The [`users.py`](target/app/api/routes/users.py) module serves the logged-in user's own resource, exposing a `GET` handler that returns the current user's profile with a fresh token and a `PUT` handler that updates it [[target/app/api/routes/users.py]]. Before persisting any change, the update handler runs uniqueness guards on both the incoming username and email, raising HTTP 400 if either is already taken by another account [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]]. Both handlers issue a new JWT on every successful request, so the token in the response always reflects the latest state of the user record [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::retrieve_current_user]] [[target/app/api/routes/users.py::update_current_user]].

Profile social features live in [`profiles.py`](target/app/api/routes/profiles.py), which exposes three endpoints for reading a profile, following a user, and unfollowing a user [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py]]. The follow and unfollow handlers share the same dependency set — a resolved `Profile`, the current authenticated `User`, and a `ProfilesRepository` — and both apply a self-referential guard that rejects requests where the caller and target are the same account [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]] [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::unsubscribe_from_user]]. The follow handler additionally raises HTTP 400 if the profile is already being followed, while the unfollow handler raises HTTP 400 if it is not currently followed, making the two mirror images of each other [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::follow_for_user]] [[target/app/api/routes/profiles.py::unsubscribe_from_user]].

Article endpoints are encapsulated in the [`articles`](target/app/api/routes/articles) sub-package, which is itself composed of three modules unified by its own `api.py` assembly point [[target/app/api/routes/articles]]. The `articles_resource` module owns the five core CRUD operations — list with filters, create, retrieve, update, and delete — where update and delete additionally enforce an ownership check through a route-level dependency before any mutation is allowed [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::update_article_by_slug]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_resource.py::delete_article_by_slug]]. The `articles_common` module covers the authenticated feed endpoint and the favourite/unfavourite pair, with both favourite handlers raising HTTP 400 when the requested state already matches the current one [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::mark_article_as_favorite]] [[target/app/api/routes/articles/articles_common.py::remove_article_from_favorites]].

Comment endpoints are handled by [`comments.py`](target/app/api/routes/comments.py), which defines three handlers for listing, creating, and deleting comments on a specific article [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py]]. Listing accepts anonymous callers while creation requires authentication and returns HTTP 201; deletion requires the caller to own the comment, enforced by a route-level dependency, and returns HTTP 204 with no body [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::list_comments_for_article]] [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::create_comment_for_article]] [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py::delete_comment_from_article]]. Across all three handlers, article and comment objects are resolved through path-based dependencies so the handler bodies receive already-resolved domain objects rather than raw path parameters [[target/app/api/routes/comments.py]].

Finally, [`tags.py`](target/app/api/routes/tags.py) exposes a single publicly accessible `GET /api/tags` endpoint that fetches every tag from the data store via an injected `TagsRepository` and returns them wrapped in a `TagsInList` response model, with no authentication required and no exceptions raised within the handler body [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py]] [[target/app/api/routes/tags.py::get_all_tags]].

The `settings` package is the central configuration system for the application, organising every runtime parameter into a layered hierarchy of Pydantic models that can be composed and overridden per deployment environment [[target/app/core/settings]].

The package initialiser marks the directory as a Python package, making all settings submodules importable by the rest of the application [[target/app/core/settings/__init__.py]]. The foundation is laid in [`base.py`](target/app/core/settings/base.py), which defines `AppEnvTypes`, an enum enumerating the three recognised deployment contexts — `prod`, `dev`, and `test` — and `BaseAppSettings`, a Pydantic `BaseSettings` subclass that reads field values from environment variables or a `.env` file and defaults `app_env` to `AppEnvTypes.prod` so the application assumes a production context unless told otherwise [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::AppEnvTypes]] [[target/app/core/settings/base.py::BaseAppSettings]].

Built on top of that foundation, [`app.py`](target/app/core/settings/app.py) defines `AppSettings`, which consolidates every setting the web server, database, authentication, and logging subsystems require into a single Pydantic model [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. It requires a `database_url` typed as `PostgresDsn` and a `secret_key` typed as `SecretStr`, meaning the application cannot start without those two values being explicitly supplied [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. The `fastapi_kwargs` property packages the seven FastAPI-relevant fields into a plain dictionary ready to be unpacked directly into the FastAPI constructor, and `configure_logging` wires the root logger and each named Uvicorn logger through Loguru's `InterceptHandler` so all log records flow through a single sink [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]]. An inner `Config` class enables `validate_assignment`, ensuring Pydantic enforces type constraints on fields even after the object has been constructed [[target/app/core/settings/app.py::AppSettings]].

The three environment-specific modules each extend `AppSettings` with targeted overrides. `DevAppSettings` enables `debug`, raises `logging_level` to `logging.DEBUG`, retitles the application for development, and reads environment variables from a `.env` file, while inheriting the complete set of database, security, routing, and logging fields unchanged [[target/app/core/settings/development.py::DevAppSettings]]. `ProdAppSettings` inherits all fields without modification and distinguishes itself solely by pointing `env_file` at `prod.env` and carrying the `AppEnvTypes.prod` default on `app_env`, making it the active settings object in production [[target/app/core/settings/production.py::ProdAppSettings]]. `TestAppSettings` overrides `debug`, `title`, `secret_key`, the connection pool limits, and `logging_level` to produce deterministic and self-contained test runs, but still requires `database_url` to be supplied externally via an environment variable rather than hardcoding a default [[target/app/core/settings/test.py::TestAppSettings]].

Taken together, the package provides a single, coherent configuration contract — defined once in `AppSettings` and specialised in each leaf class — so that the application can be started in any of its three known environments simply by selecting the appropriate settings class [[target/app/core/settings/app.py]] [[target/app/core/settings/development.py]] [[target/app/core/settings/production.py]] [[target/app/core/settings/test.py]].

The `queries` package is the database query layer for the application, providing both a pre-built SQL query executor and a set of typed table references for constructing programmatic queries [[target/app/db/queries]]. The [`__init__.py`](target/app/db/queries/__init__.py) file contains no code of its own, existing only to mark the directory as a Python package [[target/app/db/queries/__init__.py]].

The central query object is assembled in [`queries.py`](target/app/db/queries/queries.py), which uses `aiosql` to parse all SQL files from the adjacent `sql` subdirectory at import time, producing a single shared `queries` object whose attributes correspond to each named SQL statement [[target/app/db/queries/queries.py]]. The `asyncpg` driver adapter is specified during this initialisation, so every query is immediately compatible with the async database connection used throughout the application, and no further registration is needed anywhere else [[target/app/db/queries/queries.py]].

The companion module [`tables.py`](target/app/db/queries/tables.py) handles the programmatic side of database access, defining the pypika table references used to build dynamic queries [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]]. It introduces a `Parameter` subclass that formats placeholders as `$1`, `$2`, etc., matching the positional syntax expected by `asyncpg` [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Parameter]]. On top of that, `TypedTable` extends pypika's `Table` with a `__table__` attribute that lets each subclass resolve its own database table name without requiring construction-time arguments [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::TypedTable]]. Five concrete table classes are defined — `Users`, `Articles`, `Tags`, `ArticlesToTags`, and `Favorites` — each carrying typed field annotations that mirror their respective database columns [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Users]] [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Articles]] [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Tags]] [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::ArticlesToTags]] [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py::Favorites]]. Each class is instantiated once at module level, so the rest of the codebase imports these singletons directly rather than constructing new table references on every use [[target/app/db/queries/tables.py]].

The `repositories` package is the complete data-access layer of the application, grouping every database interaction into a set of focused repository classes organised around the application's core domain objects [[target/app/db/repositories]]. An empty `__init__.py` marks the directory as a Python package without exposing any symbols of its own [[target/app/db/repositories/__init__.py]].

All domain-specific repositories share a single foundation defined in `base.py`: `BaseRepository` accepts an asyncpg `Connection` at construction time, stores it as `_conn`, and exposes it through a read-only `connection` property, giving every subclass a uniform, injection-based interface to the database without duplicating connection management [[target/app/db/repositories/base.py]].

User records are handled by `UsersRepository`, which inherits from `BaseRepository` and covers the full user lifecycle through four async methods: `get_user_by_email` and `get_user_by_username` raise `EntityDoesNotExist` when no row is found, `create_user` hashes the password before inserting within a transaction, and `update_user` merges optional field overrides onto the current stored state before writing [[target/app/db/repositories/users.py::UsersRepository]].

Profile and follower-graph concerns are separated into `ProfilesRepository`, which constructs an internal `UsersRepository` on the same connection so user-level lookups remain available without duplication [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. Its `get_profile_by_username` method assembles a `Profile` from raw user data and optionally resolves the requesting user's follow state via `is_user_following_for_another_user`, while the symmetric pair `add_user_into_followers` and `remove_user_from_followers` mutate the follow graph inside database transactions [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py::ProfilesRepository]]. A `UserLike` type alias unioning `User` and `Profile` lets those mutation methods accept either domain type as input [[target/app/db/repositories/profiles.py]].

Tag persistence is the responsibility of `TagsRepository`, which exposes exactly two async methods: `get_all_tags` returns every stored tag as a flat list of strings, and `create_tags_that_dont_exist` upserts any new tags by delegating to the shared `queries` object with one `{"tag": tag}` dictionary per input entry [[target/app/db/repositories/tags.py::TagsRepository]].

The most structurally complex repository is `ArticlesRepository`, which holds internal references to both `ProfilesRepository` and `TagsRepository` on the same connection to avoid redundant connection handling [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]]. Write operations — `create_article`, `update_article`, `delete_article`, `add_article_into_favorites`, and `remove_article_from_favorites` — all execute inside transactions, with creation additionally upsert-linking tags through the private `_link_article_with_tags` helper [[target/app/db/repositories/articles.py::ArticlesRepository]].
